The root problem: a timeout is an *ambiguous* outcome, not a failure — the charge may have gone through on the processor's side even though your request didn't get a response. Any retry design's real job is resolving that ambiguity safely, not just "try again."

Recommendation:
- Generate an idempotency key per checkout attempt and reuse the *same* key on every retry of that attempt, so the processor collapses duplicate requests into the original charge instead of billing twice.
- On timeout, before retrying, query the processor for that key's actual status (Stripe, e.g., lets you look up a PaymentIntent by idempotency key). Only retry if it's genuinely unresolved.
- Do the retry (bounded attempts, backoff) in a background job, not inline in the request that the customer is waiting on. Return the customer a "processing" state instead of blocking the HTTP request or declaring failure.
- Only surface "payment failed" after retries are exhausted and the processor has confirmed a real decline/error — not on a timeout.

The one decision that actually forks this: **sync inline retry vs. async job + webhook reconciliation.** Inline is simpler but ties up the request thread and still risks a second timeout looking identical to the first. Async is more moving parts (a queue, a job, a way to notify the customer/order when it resolves) but matches how processors actually report final state (webhooks) and is what avoids the "customer sees failed, checkout row says pending forever" split you're likely hitting now. I'd go async.

Left out: the actual retry count/backoff schedule, and how the "processing" state gets pushed to the customer (poll vs. webhook-driven UI update) — that's the next layer down once you pick sync vs. async.

Depends on what's under the product catalog today — what database is it in, and roughly how many products?

The default I'd reach for: Postgres full-text search. A generated `tsvector` column combining name + description, GIN-indexed, ranked with `ts_rank`; add `pg_trgm` for typo-tolerant partial matches on short queries. Frontend debounces keystrokes and hits a `/search?q=` endpoint that paginates results. No new infrastructure, and the index stays current automatically on writes.

The one fork that matters: if you're already running Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, or you'll need relevance tuning, faceted filtering, or typo tolerance at real scale, build against that instead — same query contract, different backend. For most "type a few words, match name/description" catalogs, Postgres is the right starting point and you upgrade only if it falls short.

What I'd leave for the next level down: the tsvector weighting between name and description, debounce/query-param shape, and pagination/ranking details.

Direct-to-object-storage upload via presigned URLs, not proxied through your app server. Phone photos run 3-12MB each; routing that through your API server just to relay it to S3 burns server capacity and hits mobile upload timeouts for no benefit.

Flow: client asks your API for a presigned PUT URL (scoped to a temp/user-keyed prefix), uploads the file straight to the bucket, then tells your API "here's the object key" to attach once the listing is saved. Do the resize/compress client-side before upload — cap to a max dimension (e.g. 2000px) via canvas or a library — since that's what actually shortens upload time on cellular, versus doing it server-side after the fact. Heavier processing (thumbnail generation, HEIC to JPEG conversion, moderation) belongs server-side, async, triggered off the storage-write event, so the upload response isn't blocked on it.

The other real fork: orphan handling. Uploads happen before the listing form is submitted, so you need a pending state — photos land in a scratch prefix, get attached to the listing record on save, and anything never attached gets garbage-collected on a TTL.

Left out: multi-photo reordering/cover-photo selection, moderation policy, and resumable uploads for flaky connections — worth a follow-up if any of those matter here.

Two different mechanisms are needed here, split along the same purity line the spec already draws.

**Per-cycle alerts (most of the list)** — `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid` are already surfaced as `result.guardrail` each cycle. The pseudocode's `alert(...)` call for `quota_exceeded` generalizes directly: the supervisor just fires on `result.guardrail` after each cycle, same spot.

**Consecutive-cycle alerts** — `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned two cycles, pace error >15% for two cycles need a streak counter. The fork: put those counters in the supervisor (ad hoc, outside `govern()`) or fold them into the persisted controller `state` and let `govern()` emit them as part of its pure decision, like `feed_stale`'s existing three-cycle fallback already does. Go with the latter — it's the pattern the spec already uses, and "Core purity" is explicit that this is what keeps the guardrail logic on the unit-test/simulation ladder. Ad hoc supervisor counters would be the one piece of alerting logic invisible to the simulation harness.

**Heartbeat missed** is the odd one out — it fires exactly when the supervisor didn't run, so it can't come from inside the loop. That has to be an external watchdog: a dead-man's-switch check (e.g. Cronitor/PagerDuty heartbeat, or a Prometheus absent() rule) watching the last-cycle timestamp the supervisor persists each run.

Left out: actual alert transport/dedup (paging vs. Slack vs. ticket, and whether repeated firings collapse) — that's downstream of this and not implied by the spec.

This service already has one property that makes this easy: every write funnels through a single function, `write()` in db.js:13-26, which opens and commits the transaction. - **DB-level**: have `write()` run `SET LOCAL app.user_id = $1` right after `BEGIN` (db.js:16), and put an `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` trigger on each writable table that appends `(table, row_id, action, old row as jsonb, new row as jsonb, current_setting('app.user_id'), now())` to an append-only `audit_log`.

Cache-aside on the DB queries feeding the page, keyed by product ID (plus locale/currency if those vary output), backed by Redis with a short TTL as a safety net. On a request: check cache, miss falls through to the DB, populate cache, return. That collapses the 900ms to a cache hit's latency (single-digit ms) for the common case, and it's the standard fit since the bottleneck is reads that repeat heavily across users.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

Raw results are safer (personalization, A/B tests, currency still apply at render time) but leave rendering cost on every request. Full-page caching is faster but only works if the page is the same for every visitor hitting that key. Pick raw query result caching unless you've confirmed the page is truly visitor-agnostic.

**Invalidation** — TTL-only (simple, but stale data for up to the TTL window) vs. event-driven invalidation on product write (fresher, but requires wiring cache busting into every write path, including admin tools and batch jobs). Pick TTL-only first (e.g., 60s) and add event-driven invalidation later only if staleness after a price/inventory edit actually causes problems.

Enforce it at the edge, in front of `/v1` (gateway or middleware), keyed by client identity — API key or auth token, not source IP, since IP is unreliable behind NAT/shared proxies. Use a token-bucket counter and return 429 with a `Retry-After` header when a client exceeds its bucket.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Where the counter state lives.** In-process/local counters are cheap and add no latency, but each app instance only sees its own slice of traffic, so a client hitting multiple instances can blow past the intended limit — which is exactly the failure mode you're trying to fix. A shared store (Redis, via `INCR`+TTL or a Lua script for atomicity) enforces one true global count per client at the cost of a network round-trip per request. Given the problem is one client degrading the shared endpoint, go with the shared store — correctness matters more than the extra hop.
2. **Algorithm.** Fixed window is simplest but lets a client burst up to 2x the limit at window boundaries. Token bucket (or sliding-window log) smooths that out and still allows short legitimate bursts without raising the sustained rate — the standard choice here.

Left out: the actual per-tier limit values and whether internal/privileged callers get a separate bucket or bypass entirely.

The fork is push vs. poll, and it depends on how the underlying data changes.

If updates come from discrete events (new alert, deploy, status flip), push it: backend publishes on change (Redis pub/sub, DB change stream, or just an in-process event bus) to clients over Server-Sent Events — simpler than WebSockets since it's one-directional and reconnects automatically. If the data is continuously fluctuating (CPU%, request rate), polling every 10–30s with an ETag/If-None-Match check is just as fresh in practice and avoids maintaining persistent connections.

Recommendation: SSE with a polling fallback — most ops dashboards have a mix of event-like state changes and slow-moving metrics, and SSE handles both fine while degrading gracefully if a proxy blocks it.

Left out: auth/reconnect handling on the SSE stream and how many concurrent dashboard viewers you need to support — those are the next-level decisions once you pick a transport.

The customer-facing bug is a symptom: a timeout means "unknown outcome," not "failed," and if you're currently treating it as failed you're probably either double-charging on retry or wrongly telling people it didn't go through.

**Fix underneath both forks:** always send an idempotency key with the charge, generated once per checkout attempt (not per HTTP call), and reuse that same key on every retry. The processor then returns the original charge's result instead of creating a second one. Give timeouts their own status distinct from declines, and only retry that status — never retry a confirmed decline.

**Fork 1 — where the retry happens.** Inline: retry the same request once or twice with short backoff before responding to the customer. Simple, but only works if your timeout budget leaves room for it. Async: mark the charge "pending," return immediately, retry from a background job/queue, and update the order once resolved. Needed if timeouts are already near your request deadline — and it's what lets you stop showing "failed" for something that's just slow.

**Fork 2 — the safety net.** A periodic reconciliation job that queries the processor for any charge still "pending"/"unknown" past N minutes and resolves it. This is what catches the case where the retry itself times out or the worker dies mid-flight — the idempotency key + retry path alone won't.

Left for the next level: backoff/attempt limits, the full pending/succeeded/failed state machine, webhook vs. poll for resolving pending charges, and what copy you show the customer while it's in flight.

The core issue: a timeout means you don't know if the charge went through on the processor's side, so retrying blindly risks a double charge, and failing blindly risks a false decline the customer didn't cause.

Recommended shape:
- Tag each checkout attempt with an idempotency key (one per logical purchase, not per HTTP call) and pass it to the gateway on every retry — the gateway then dedupes internally instead of creating a second charge, and returns the original outcome if it already completed.
- On timeout, write the charge as `pending`/`unknown`, never `failed`. Before retrying, reconcile: ask the gateway for the status of that idempotency key/reference — if it actually succeeded, mark it paid and stop; only retry if it's genuinely unresolved or declined.
- Do the retry+reconcile loop in a background job with backoff, not inline in the request — the customer sees "processing" and the UI polls or gets a webhook, rather than the request hanging on N retries before answering.

The two decisions that actually fork this: whether idempotency keys are generated client-side (survives a page refresh) or server-side (simpler, but a refresh becomes a new attempt), and how long the customer waits on "processing" before you show any failure state at all. Retry counts, backoff curve, and webhook plumbing are the level below that.

Cache-aside in front of the DB is the right default: on a page load, check Redis (or similar) for the product data by key, and on a miss, query the DB and populate the cache. Two decisions actually fork the design:

**What you cache** — raw query results vs. the fully rendered page/fragment. Query-result caching (keyed by product ID) is the safer default unless you know the page is fully static per product.

**How you invalidate** — TTL-only vs. event-driven. TTL is simpler: set an expiry matched to how stale the data is allowed to get (minutes, typically) and let it lapse. Event-driven invalidation (bust the key on every write to that product) is more accurate but means touching every write path. For product pages, TTL-only is usually enough unless price/stock correctness is strict enough that a few minutes of staleness is unacceptable.

One thing worth building in regardless: a stampede guard (lock or short jittered TTL) so a hot key's expiry doesn't send a burst of concurrent requests to the DB at once.

What's DB and cache layer are you actually running, and is any part of the page personalized per user? That determines which fork applies.

Identify the client by API key (or auth token), not IP — shared IPs/NAT make IP-based limits punish innocent users while letting a determined client rotate around them. Enforce it at the edge (reverse proxy or gateway, e.g. nginx `limit_req`, Envoy, or a gateway like Kong) rather than in application code, so the offending traffic never reaches `/v1`'s workers at all. Use a token-bucket algorithm (allows bursts, smooths sustained abuse) with per-key limits, backed by Redis if you're running more than one instance so the count is shared; return `429` with a `Retry-After` header on rejection.

The fork that actually matters here: if you're single-instance, an in-memory bucket is fine and simpler; if you're horizontally scaled, you need the shared Redis counter or each instance's local limit lets the client burst through under the aggregate cap. Tuning the actual rate/burst thresholds per client tier is the next layer down.

Looking at `payments.js` and `PROVIDER.md`: a timeout there is explicitly "unknown, never failed" per the vendor, and `charge()` already accepts no `Idempotency-Key` even though the API supports one. That's the whole fix — a timeout should trigger a retry with the *same* idempotency key, not a failure response.

**Approach**: before calling `charge()`, derive a stable idempotency key from `order.id` (one charge per order, so the order id itself is the key — no counter needed) and pass it as `Idempotency-Key`. In `checkout.js`, catch timeout/network errors separately from 4xx: on timeout, retry the same call (same key, 2-3 attempts, short backoff) since the vendor guarantees a byte-identical replay of the original result, whatever it was. Only a real rejection (4xx from the vendor) or exhausted retries becomes a customer-visible failure.

The two decisions that actually fork this:

1. **Where the key lives.** It must survive a process crash between "charge sent" and "order updated," or a restart-then-retry double-charges. So write the idempotency key (just `order.id`) to the row *before* calling `charge()`, not only hold it in a local variable — that's what makes retry safe across restarts, not just within one request.
2. **Sync vs. async retry.** A few timeouts a day is low volume and the customer is sitting on checkout, so retrying inline (bounded loop, request stays open) is simpler than marking the order "processing" and reconciling via a background job. Move to async only if retries themselves start timing out often enough to matter.

Left out: a reconciliation job for the case where all inline retries also time out (order stuck "pending" with a charge that may have gone through) — that's the next layer down, not needed for the common case.

At 38k rows on Postgres already, don't bring in a separate search service — use Postgres full-text search:

- Add a generated `tsvector` column on `products` combining `name` (weighted higher) and `description`, with a GIN index on it.
- Add a `GET /products/search?q=` route that runs `plainto_tsquery` against that column, ordered by `ts_rank`, reusing the same pagination shape the `/` route already has.

The fork that matters: plain `tsvector`/`ts_rank` handles "type a few words, match name/description" well but does whole-word stemmed matching, not prefix-as-you-type or typo tolerance — if the UI wants results while the user is still typing, use `to_tsquery` with `:*` prefix matching on the last term instead of `plainto_tsquery`. If you need fuzzy/misspelling tolerance too, that's `pg_trgm`, a second index and query path — worth doing only if you know users mistype.

**Recommendation:** upload directly from the client to object storage (S3/GCS/R2) via a short-lived presigned URL — don't proxy the file through your app server. Phone photos run 3–15MB each (HEIC or JPEG); routing that through your API burns server memory/CPU and hits timeouts on bad mobile connections.

Flow: app server creates a `listing_photos` row (`status=pending`) and a presigned PUT URL, the client uploads straight to the bucket, then either the client calls a `/photos/:id/complete` endpoint or an S3 event notification flips the row to `ready` and enqueues a thumbnail job.

Two decisions actually fork this design:

1. **Resize on client or server.** Phone cameras produce 12MP+ HEIC/JPEG — if nothing caps that, you're storing and serving full-res originals for what's usually a thumbnail grid. Cheapest fix: resize/re-encode client-side before upload (cap long edge to ~2000px, convert HEIC to JPEG). Still generate thumbnails server-side async as a backstop, since you can't trust client resize alone (web uploads, API misuse, old app versions).
2. **Moderation gate.** Decide whether photos go live immediately or sit `pending` until a moderation/virus check clears — matters if listings are public marketplace content.

Left out at this depth: multi-photo ordering/reordering state, resumable upload for flaky mobile connections (tus or S3 multipart), and cache/CDN invalidation on photo replace. Straightforward once the above is in place — say if you want any of those detailed.

Build it as an extension of `govern()`'s pure output, not a bolt-on in the supervisor:

Have `govern()` return the full set of conditions it detected that cycle (all eight observability triggers, each computed from `state`/`inputs`), not just the single winning guardrail. The supervisor's loop stays close to the pseudocode, but instead of `if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded": alert(...)`, it iterates `result.conditions` and calls `alert()` for each newly-true one.

Two decisions actually fork this design:

1. **Guardrails pick the cap; conditions drive alerts — these can't be the same field.** "First match wins" (line 46) is correct for deciding the cap, but if alerting also keys off that single winning guardrail, a `floor_at_risk` condition gets silently swallowed whenever `cap_clamped` happens to win priority that cycle. The observability list (lines 64-73) is a superset of the guardrail list, so it needs its own, broader signal out of `govern()`.

2. **The three "N consecutive cycles" triggers need cross-cycle memory** (`feed_stale` past 3, cap pinned for 2, pace error >15% for 2). SPEC.md already puts exactly this kind of counter inside the persisted controller state for `feed_stale`'s own fallback (line 51-52). Extending that same pattern — streak counters live in `state`, `govern()` stays pure — keeps everything replayable by the simulation harness. Moving the counting into the supervisor instead would make alert behavior something the harness can't reproduce, which fights the core-purity rationale in the doc (lines 37-42).

`heartbeat_missed` doesn't fit either bucket: `govern()` only runs when invoked, so it can't detect its own non-execution. That has to be an external watchdog — a separate check comparing each tenant's last-recorded cycle timestamp against the 5-minute cadence.

Left out: actual alert transport (PagerDuty/Slack/etc.) and dedup/rate-limiting so a persisting condition doesn't re-fire every cycle — plumbing, not a design fork.

**Cache the expensive DB reads, not the whole request.** Put a cache-aside layer (Redis) in front of the queries that build the product page — key by product ID (+ variant/locale), read-through on miss, write to cache after the DB read. Add request coalescing (a lock/singleflight per key) so a cold key doesn't let 50 concurrent requests all hit the DB at once — that's the usual reason "caching" doesn't fix latency under load.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Personalized or not.** If the page is identical for every visitor (no per-user price/cart/recs), push the cache out to the CDN/edge and skip your app servers entirely — biggest latency win, least code. If it's personalized, cache only the shared expensive parts (product data, reviews aggregate, inventory) in Redis and compose the page around them; don't try to cache the personalized parts.
- **Staleness tolerance.** TTL-only (e.g. 30–60s) is simplest and fine if price/stock don't need to be instantly correct. If they do, invalidate the key explicitly when the product record changes (same transaction or an event handler on the write path) rather than waiting out a TTL.

Left for the next level: exact TTL, key schema, and warming — those depend on your DB/ORM and how often product data actually changes.

Key fork: what to key the limit on. Client `X-Api-Key` maps to `client_id` via the existing lookup in `routes/api.js:9-19` — key the limiter on `client_id`, not IP. IPs don't work here since clients share NAT'd addresses and single clients call from many.

Second fork: where to store counters. `app.js` runs 4 clustered workers per box with separate heaps (`app.js:4-6`), so an in-process counter only sees a quarter of one box's traffic. `redis.js` already gives every worker a shared store — reuse it for a per-`client_id` counter (`INCR` + `EXPIRE` fixed window, or a Lua script if you want atomic check-and-increment).

Enforce it inside the existing auth middleware (`routes/api.js:9`), right after `req.client` is resolved and before any Postgres call, so a hammering client gets rejected with `429` + `Retry-After` without touching the DB pool that's currently getting starved. Since that middleware already fetches `plan`, the limit can be looked up per plan instead of one global number.

Left out: burst handling (fixed window vs. token bucket), and Redis itself becoming a single point of contention/failure under this load.

Polling, not push — PLATFORM.md rules out the alternative: WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, and SSE needs a connection held open past the 10s function timeout, which frozen serverless instances with no sticky routing can't do either.

Concretely: replace the click handler in `public/dashboard.js` with a `setInterval(load, 60_000)`, since `jobs/rollup.md` says `rollup` only changes once a minute on the minute — polling faster just re-fetches identical rows (`api/metrics.js` already reads a cheap 4KB/30ms query with `no-store`, so the endpoint itself doesn't need to change). Compare the new `computed_at` to the last-seen value before calling `render()`, so a poll that lands between rollup writes doesn't re-render the DOM for no reason. Keep the refresh button if you want a manual "check now" affordance, but it can't get fresher data than the last minute mark regardless of when it's clicked.

One thing to decide: whether polls should land right after `:00` (tightest freshness) or be jittered a few seconds past it (avoids every open dashboard hammering the rollup job's write instant at once).

The real bug isn't "add retries" — it's that a timeout means *unknown outcome*, not *failed*. A bare retry on that risks double-charging the customer if the original charge actually landed.

**Design:**
1. **Idempotency key per checkout attempt** (not per HTTP call) — generate it once, send it on the initial charge and every retry of that same charge. The processor (Stripe et al.) dedupes on it server-side, so a retry either returns the original result or safely re-attempts if nothing was created.
2. **Retry only on timeout/network errors**, never on declines — a decline is terminal; retrying it just re-runs the same rejection and wastes the customer's time.
3. **Inline retry with short backoff** (e.g. 3 attempts, capped ~5–10s total) since the customer is waiting on the request. If it's still unresolved after that, don't show "payment failed" — show "confirming payment" and resolve the final state out-of-band via webhook/poll, since the charge may still succeed on the processor's side after your request gave up.

The fork that matters: **inline synchronous retry** (simple, customer waits a few extra seconds) vs. **mark-pending + async resolution** (customer sees a pending state, order finalizes later via webhook). At "a few times a day," inline is enough — go async only if timeouts start taking longer than a checkout page will tolerate.

**Recommendation:** do it in Postgres, not a separate search engine. Add a generated `tsvector` column on `products` (name weighted `'A'`, description `'B'`), a GIN index on it, and a new `GET /products/search?q=` route in `routes/products.js` that runs `websearch_to_tsquery` against it and orders by `ts_rank`. At 38k rows growing by a few hundred a month, that's comfortably within what a GIN-indexed tsvector handles with room to spare — no new service, no sync job, no extra failure mode.

The one real fork: **Postgres full-text vs. an external engine** (Elasticsearch/Algolia/Meilisearch). Those buy you typo-tolerance and relevance tuning out of the box, but at this scale they're infrastructure you'd be running just to search 38k rows — not worth it unless traffic or dataset size is expected to jump an order of magnitude next year.

Left out: typo/fuzzy matching. `websearch_to_tsquery` does stemming and phrase logic but won't forgive misspellings — if that matters, `pg_trgm` similarity as a secondary fallback is the next thing to add, not the first.

Direct-to-S3 via signed PUT, not through the app/nginx path — the pieces are already staged for exactly this: `storage.js`'s `signedUrl` helper already supports `method: 'PUT'`, and the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com`. That also sidesteps the real blocker: nginx's `client_max_body_size 1m` is shared with the payments listener on purpose (cited in their PCI paperwork, per-location overrides already declined), and phone camera JPEGs routinely run 3–8MB — so proxying bytes through the app was never viable regardless.

Flow: a route (e.g. `POST /:id/photos`) mints a server-side key like `listings/${id}/${uuid}.jpg` and returns `storage.signedUrl(key, {method: 'PUT'})`; the client PUTs bytes straight to S3; a follow-up call runs `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` to append to `photo_keys`, mirroring the existing invoice read pattern in `routes/listings.js`.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Key ownership** — the key must be generated server-side from the listing id, never accepted from the client, or a seller can overwrite another listing's photos.
- **Size/type enforcement** — a bare presigned PUT can't cap file size or content-type. If that matters, it's a presigned POST policy (different signing helper, supports `content-length-range`) rather than PUT.

Left out: thumbnailing, EXIF orientation/GPS stripping, multi-photo ordering — depends on how the listing UI renders them.

Two things fork this design, and both come straight from constraints already in the spec:

**1. Multi-cycle conditions need counters the pure core doesn't have.** `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, and `config_invalid` are one-shot — `govern()`'s `result.guardrail` on a single cycle is enough. But `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned for two, and pace error above 15% for two are consecutive-cycle conditions, and `govern()` is deliberately stateless of I/O and only emits one guardrail per call. Don't fold this into the tenant's controller state — that state is what the simulation harness replays byte-for-byte against recorded production days, and alert thresholds are ops-tunable knobs that will change independently of control logic. Keep a separate small alert-tracking record per tenant (last N guardrails/cap values, consecutive counts) that the supervisor updates right where it already does `apply_cap` / `persist_state`, and evaluate the eight conditions against that record after each cycle.

**2. "Heartbeat missed" can't be raised by the loop, because the loop didn't run.** That one needs an external watchdog: something outside the five-minute loop that checks, per tenant, whether `persist_state` was written recently — a dead-man's-switch (Prometheus absent-alert, Cronitor, or a scheduled check against the persisted cycle timestamp) firing if it's older than one interval.

Everything else is just replacing the pseudocode's single `alert("quota exceeded", tenant)` with a call for each of the eight conditions, keyed by `(tenant, condition)` so repeats don't repage every five minutes.

What do you already page through — PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Slack, something else? That decides what `alert()` actually calls.

Every write in this service already funnels through one function — `db.write()` in `db.js:13`, which already opens a transaction and returns the row. That's the interception point: append an `audit_log` insert inside that same transaction, so an audit row is never silently skipped and never orphaned from the write it describes.

**Who**: `req.user` is resolved once, in `sessionUser` (`auth.js:5`), before any route runs. Rather than threading `req` through every route into `db.write()`, stash `{id, email}` in `AsyncLocalStorage` at the top of `sessionUser` and have `write()` read it — no call-site signature changes.

**What**: `write()` only sees raw SQL text, so it can't infer table/action reliably. With just four write call sites today (`accounts.js` PATCH/DELETE, `orders.js` POST/PATCH), pass a small explicit metadata object — `{table: 'accounts', action: 'update'}` — at each call rather than regex-parsing the query. Regex-parsing SQL to infer intent is the kind of fragile magic that breaks silently the first time someone writes a multi-table statement.

**Old/new values**: `RETURNING *` only gives the after-state. For a real diff, `write()` should `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` the target row before running the mutation, inside the same transaction, then store both `before` and `after` as jsonb. That's one extra query per write — worth it, since "who changed what" means column-level values, not just "an update happened."

`audit_log` schema: `id, occurred_at default now(), actor_user_id, actor_email, table_name, row_id, action, before jsonb, after jsonb`. Make it insert-only at the DB level (revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` from the app role) so compliance can trust it wasn't edited after the fact.

Left out: retention/export policy, and what to do if a second write path ever bypasses `db.write()` — worth a lint rule or code-review convention once this exists, not part of the audit-log design itself.

Two things stand out from `db.js`, `middleware/security.js`, and `CDN.md`: the CDN is already in front and honors *only* origin `Cache-Control` headers, and `security.js` slaps `no-store` on every route — including `/p`, which is fully anonymous and identical for every visitor. That blanket header is why the edge hit rate is 0%, and it's the actual bug, not a missing cache layer.

**Recommendation:** split `security.js` into two policies. Keep `/account` exactly as-is (`no-store` — that's the audit fix and must stay). Give `/p` a real `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` instead of inheriting the lockdown. Because the CDN already respects origin headers with no path rules of its own, this is a one-file change that turns the existing edge into a cache for product pages — a hit skips the DB, and the 600ms `relatedProducts` join, entirely.

**The one real fork:** the page mixes two freshness rates. `productBySlug`/`relatedProducts` are catalog data that changes a few times a day; `stockFor` moves with every order. Caching the whole rendered page under one TTL means picking a side:
- Cache the whole page at ~60s (stock can show up to a minute stale). Standard for ecommerce "in stock" badges, zero extra moving parts.
- Or split stock into its own small endpoint that's fetched uncached (client-side or edge-side include) while the cacheable page carries only product+related, the 640ms part. Worth it only if the page shows something stock-sensitive like an exact "3 left" count.

I'd start with the first — one TTL, one header change — and only carve out stock separately if staleness there turns out to matter.

Next level down (not decided here): exact TTL/`stale-while-revalidate` values, whether to add a Redis cache in front of `relatedProducts` for edge-cold requests, and whether admin edits should purge the CDN cache or just wait out the TTL.

Read the code — this is Express behind a 4-worker cluster (`app.js:7`), with a shared Redis (`redis.js`) already used for sessions, and an auth middleware (`routes/api.js:9-19`) that resolves every request to a `client_id` before it reaches the handlers. That maps cleanly onto the fix.

**Recommendation:** a per-`client_id` token bucket, enforced in that same auth middleware right after `req.client` is set, backed by the existing Redis instance (one Lua script per request, `EVAL`, so the check-and-consume is atomic — plain `INCR`+`EXPIRE` isn't, and you need atomicity since 4 workers × N boxes are hitting the same key concurrently). Bucket key: `ratelimit:{client_id}`. Over limit → `429` with `Retry-After`, before the Postgres query ever runs.

Two things actually fork the design:

- **Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The comment in `api.js:6-8` already says IP is unreliable here (shared NAT, multi-address clients), and `client_id` is sitting right there from the key lookup — this one's basically forced by the existing code.
- **Scope: one bucket for all of `/v1`, not per-route.** Since the complaint is "hammering /v1" generally, a single client-wide cap is the right first cut. If it turns out the actual damage is concentrated on `POST /reports` (the one hitting Postgres with writes) rather than the `GET`, a tighter sub-limit on that route is the natural follow-up, not the starting point.

Left out, for later: what the limit/burst size should be per plan tier, and what happens on Redis unavailability (fail-open vs fail-closed) — that's a real tradeoff but not one to guess at without knowing your uptime/abuse tolerance.

Push from the server rather than having clients poll. For a one-way display like an ops dashboard, Server-Sent Events (the browser's `EventSource`) is the sweet spot: plain HTTP, auto-reconnect built in, far simpler than WebSockets to build and operate. Reach for WebSockets only if the dashboard needs to send something back (e.g., acknowledging an alert), not just display state.

The fork is what's actually changing on the backend. If there's a process that already knows when data changes (a queue consumer, a DB trigger, a metrics ingester), have it push diffs to connected clients over SSE. If changes are cheap to compute and infrequent, a 15–30s client-side poll is honestly simpler to build and debug, and satisfies "no manual refresh" just as well — push only pays off once poll volume or staleness becomes a real problem.

What's the dashboard's current stack?

Don't treat a timeout as a failure — it means "unknown," since the charge may have actually gone through upstream and only the response was lost. Retrying blindly on that assumption is how you get double charges.

The fix has two parts:
- **Idempotency key** per logical charge attempt (e.g. `order_id` + attempt number), sent identically on every retry, so the processor coalesces duplicates instead of creating a second charge.
- **Resolve before retry**: on timeout, check the charge's actual status (poll the processor by that idempotency key, or wait for its webhook) before deciding to retry. Only retry if it's genuinely unresolved/failed, with a small bounded backoff (e.g. 3 attempts, 2s/4s/8s + jitter).

The fork that matters: **sync inline retry vs. async reconciliation**. Since this is "a few times a day," don't hold the customer's request open through retries — accept the charge attempt, return "processing" (not "failed") to the customer, and resolve/retry in a background job driven by processor webhooks or a poll loop. That also fixes the UX bug on its own: "payment failed" should only ever be shown for a confirmed decline, not a timeout.

Left out: backoff tuning specifics, alerting on charges stuck in "uncertain" past N minutes, and processor-specific idempotency semantics (Stripe vs. others differ slightly) — worth nailing down once you pick a processor.

Build it on Postgres full-text search, not a separate search service — at 38k rows and "a few hundred a month" growth, Elasticsearch/Algolia/Meilisearch is operational overhead you don't need yet.

Add a generated `tsvector` column combining name and description with weights (name ranked higher), backed by a GIN index:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

Then a new route using `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles multi-word user input more forgivingly than `plainto_tsquery`) ordered by `ts_rank`, still filtered on `active`.

The one real fork: exact/prefix full-text matching alone will miss typos and partial words (e.g., "hoodei" won't match "hoodie"). If that matters for this catalog, pair it with `pg_trgm` (trigram similarity) for fuzzy fallback — still Postgres, just a second GIN index. Worth deciding now since it changes the query logic, not just the index.

Left out at this depth: pagination/ranking tuning, autocomplete-as-you-type (a separate, cheaper endpoint), and synonym handling — those are next-level details once the basic approach is picked.

Direct-to-storage upload: client requests a presigned URL from your API, uploads the file straight to object storage (S3/R2/GCS), then confirms completion to your API so it can attach the resulting image ID to the listing. This keeps multi-MB phone photos off your app servers entirely — no request body limits or worker memory tied up on file bytes.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:

1. **Where resizing happens.** Do client-side downscale/compress before upload (fast feedback, less bandwidth, but inconsistent across devices/browsers) vs. upload the original and run an async worker on the storage-complete event to generate thumbnail/medium/full variants and strip EXIF (including GPS — sellers' photos otherwise leak home addresses). I'd do both: a light client-side resize cap (e.g. downscale anything over ~2000px before upload) plus a server-side worker for the real variant set, since you can't trust the client alone.

2. **When the listing becomes valid.** Photos should attach via a "pending" state until the storage-complete webhook fires and processing succeeds, not on client-reported success — otherwise a flaky upload leaves a listing pointing at a broken image.

Left out: retry/resumable upload for flaky mobile networks, and moderation/content-scanning pipeline — worth a follow-up if either matters here.

Alerting should live entirely in the supervisor, as a side effect after `govern()` returns — never inside the pure core. `govern()` already tells you the guardrail that fired each cycle, so single-cycle alerts (`quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`) are a direct mapping from `result.guardrail` to `alert()`, same as the pseudocode already shows for `quota_exceeded`.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Where "consecutive cycles" gets counted.** Conditions like `feed_stale` past three cycles, a cap pinned for two, or pace error over 15% for two need memory across cycles. That counting can go into `govern()`'s persisted state (a `stale_streak`, `pinned_streak`, `pace_error_streak` field it increments/resets each call) or into a separate supervisor-side tracker. Putting it in `govern()`'s state keeps it pure and deterministic — the simulation harness can replay a shadow week and assert the exact same streak counts and alert-worthy flags came out, which is the property the spec leans on hardest. A supervisor-side tracker duplicates that logic somewhere untested by the replay harness. Fold the streak counters into state.

2. **Heartbeat missed can't be detected from inside the loop.** If the loop doesn't run, nothing inside it fires. This has to be an external watcher — something outside the five-minute job checking "has `persist_state`/`record_cycle` advanced in the last N minutes per tenant" (a dead-man's-switch check, e.g. a separate cron or your monitoring system's staleness alert on the last-cycle timestamp).

Left out at the next level down: the actual `alert()` sink (PagerDuty/Slack/etc.), dedup so a 3-cycle streak doesn't refire every cycle after the threshold, and per-tenant vs. fleet-wide alert routing.

Every write in this service already funnels through one place: `db.write()` in db.js:13-26, which wraps each call in its own `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`. That's the natural anchor, but there's a real fork on where the audit record gets written.

**Recommendation: Postgres triggers, not an app-level log in `db.write()`.**

Compliance needs "every write," not "every write that happened to go through our wrapper." Right now that's the same set of writes, but it's only true by convention — nothing stops a future migration, a one-off `psql` fix, or a different code path from writing to `accounts` or `orders` directly and leaving no trace. Triggers move the guarantee into the database itself, so it holds regardless of how the row got touched.

Concretely:
1. An append-only `audit_log` table: `id, table_name, row_id, action, actor_id, actor_email, before, after, changed_at`. Revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on it from the app's DB role so it can't be edited after the fact, only inserted into.
2. An `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger on `accounts` and `orders` that writes `row_to_json(OLD)`/`row_to_json(NEW)` into `audit_log`.
3. The "who" is the missing piece: nothing below `db.write()` currently knows about `req.user`. Fix that by having `db.write()` take the actor as a third argument — `db.write(text, params, req.user)` — and, inside the existing transaction, run `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = $1; SET LOCAL app.actor_email = $2` before the real query. The trigger reads those via `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)`. Since it's `SET LOCAL` inside the same transaction `db.write()` already opens, it's automatically scoped to that one write and cleared on commit/rollback — no cross-request leakage.
4. Every call site (routes/accounts.js:7,15, routes/orders.js:7,15) changes from `db.write(text, params)` to `db.write(text, params, req.user)`. That's the only application-code change needed — the audit capture itself lives entirely in the trigger, so new tables or new write paths only need the trigger added, not new logging code.

The one thing this doesn't solve on its own: `sessionUser` (auth.js) sets `req.user`, but if a write ever happens outside a request (a cron job, a console script), there's no `req.user` to pass — that caller needs its own actor identity convention. That's the next-level-down design decision, not blocking for this first pass.

Cache the DB result behind a key on product id (plus locale/currency if those vary the query), not the whole rendered HTML — that keeps it framework-agnostic and lets you reuse it for API responses too. Put it in Redis/Memcached with a TTL matched to how stale you can tolerate (minutes, not seconds, for things like description/images), and invalidate explicitly on write for fields that must be fresh, like price or stock.

The one fork that matters: TTL-only is simpler but risks serving stale prices; write-through invalidation is fresher but means every write path needs to know to bust the cache, and you need to handle races where an invalidation lands before the write commits. I'd default to TTL-only for content, explicit invalidation only for price/inventory.

The other thing worth building in from the start: at 900ms, an empty/expired cache under real traffic is a thundering-herd risk — many requests missing at once and hammering the DB. Add request coalescing (single-flight so only one request per key repopulates, others wait) rather than bolting it on after a fire drill.

What's your stack (Redis available? ORM/query layer)? That determines whether this is a decorator around one query function or something more involved.

Recommendation: add rate-limit middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after the auth middleware (line 19) since it already resolves `req.client.client_id` and `req.client.plan` — key the limit on `client_id`, not IP. The comment on that middleware says one client can span many addresses and several clients can share one NAT'd address, so IP-based limiting would both under-limit the abusive client and collateral-damage its neighbors.

Count in the Redis you already have (`redis.js`), not in-process. `app.js` runs 4 workers per box with nothing shared between them, so an in-memory counter would let each worker give the client its own separate quota — a client could burst 4x by hitting different workers. Redis is already the one thing every worker/box shares. Use an atomic `INCR` + `PEXPIRE` (or a small Lua script if you want it race-free in one round trip) on a key like `ratelimit:{client_id}:{window}`, and return 429 with `Retry-After` when the plan's threshold is exceeded.

Two things that genuinely fork the design, not just details:

- **Fixed window vs token bucket** — `INCR`/`EXPIRE` is a five-line fixed window but lets a client burst 2x at the window boundary; a token bucket (still doable in one Lua script) smooths that out at the cost of slightly more logic.
- **Redis down, fail open or closed** — fail open means an outage lets the hammering client back in during the exact scenario you're defending against; fail closed means a Redis blip takes down `/v1` for everyone. Given Redis is already a hard dependency for sessions, fail open is likely fine here — that dependency risk already exists.

Left out: exact per-plan limits/burst sizes, and whether this should also cap the two DB queries in `api.js` specifically (e.g. the unbounded `INSERT` on `/reports`) versus a blanket request-count limit.

Use Server-Sent Events (SSE), not WebSockets or client-side polling: the dashboard only needs one-way updates (server to browser), and SSE gives you auto-reconnect and works over plain HTTP without the connection-management overhead WebSockets require.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **How the server learns data changed** — either it subscribes to the same event/queue that writes the underlying data (push-driven, near-instant), or it polls the data source on an interval and diffs (simpler, but adds latency equal to the poll interval). Pick push-driven if the data source already emits events (DB triggers, message queue, webhook); pick interval-poll if it's just a database you'd otherwise query.
2. **What you send on update** — the full dashboard state each time, or just a diff/delta. Full state is simpler and fine unless the payload is large or updates are frequent.

Left out: auth on the SSE connection, reconnection/backoff details, and horizontal scaling (multiple server instances need a shared pub/sub like Redis to fan out events to all connected clients).

The real bug is upstream: a timeout is being treated as a decline. Fix that distinction first, then retries follow naturally.

- Generate one idempotency key per logical charge attempt, reuse it across every retry. This is non-negotiable — without it, retrying a charge that actually succeeded on the gateway's side (just slow to respond) double-charges the customer.
- On timeout, don't mark the charge "failed." Mark it "processing," then reconcile: query the gateway for that charge/idempotency key's actual status (or wait for its webhook) before deciding anything.
- Only after reconciliation confirms a genuine failure do you retry — as an async job with backoff (a few attempts, minutes apart), not inline in the customer's request. Timeouts are usually transient gateway load, so blocking the customer for a second live attempt risks a second timeout for no benefit.
- Customer-facing state becomes "processing" → "paid" or "payment failed," never a premature "failed" during the ambiguous window.

The fork that matters: idempotency key + reconcile-before-retry is mandatory; sync-vs-async retry is the other real choice, and async wins here since these are transient gateway timeouts, not something the user should sit and wait through twice.

Left out: backoff/attempt-count tuning, webhook vs. polling for reconciliation, and alerting/dead-lettering once retries are exhausted — all one level down from this.

Postgres full-text search — at 38k rows and growing by a few hundred a month, adding Elasticsearch/Algolia is unwarranted infrastructure; the `pg` pool already in `db.js` handles it natively.

Concretely: add a generated `tsvector` column to `products` that combines `name` (weight A) and `description` (weight B), with a GIN index on it, then add `GET /products/search?q=` to `routes/products.js` using `websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)` against that column, ordered by `ts_rank`. Weighting name over description means a query matching the title ranks above one that only hits the description.

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;
CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

The fork that actually matters: plain `to_tsquery` stemming won't match partial words or typos (e.g. "hoodi" won't find "hoodie"). If the product names have short/compound tokens or you expect typos, pair it with `pg_trgm` (trigram similarity index) and blend the two scores — that's the part worth prototyping against real query logs before committing to one, not something to decide upfront.

Left out: query-side concerns like debouncing/pagination on the frontend, and whether `active` filtering plus the new WHERE clause still hits the index efficiently — worth an `EXPLAIN` once real data's loaded, not a blocker to starting.

**Recommended flow:**

1. Client requests an upload slot from your backend (`POST /listings/:id/photos`), which creates a photo record in "pending" state and returns a presigned upload URL for object storage (S3/GCS/etc).
2. Client uploads directly to storage using that URL — this keeps multi-megabyte camera photos off your app server entirely.
3. Client resizes/compresses on-device before uploading (cap around 2000px, convert HEIC to JPEG) — phone camera originals run 3-10MB and mobile connections are slow and flaky, so shrinking client-side cuts upload time and failure rate.
4. Storage fires a completion event, backend marks the photo "ready" and queues a background job to generate thumbnail and display-size variants.
5. The listing UI shows photos in a "processing" state until variants exist, rather than blocking on synchronous server-side resizing.

**Key fork:** direct-to-storage (presigned URL) vs. proxying the upload through your app server. Proxying is simpler to stand up first — one endpoint takes a multipart upload — but it ties up server workers on slow mobile transfers and doubles the data movement (phone to server, then server to storage). Direct-to-storage needs a bit more setup (bucket CORS, a presigned-URL endpoint) but scales cleanly and is the standard choice once you're past a prototype.

**Mobile-specific details worth getting right up front:** retry/resume on dropped connections (very common mid-upload on mobile), respecting EXIF orientation (camera photos are often stored sideways with a rotation flag), and HEIC (iPhone's default format, which many browsers and image libraries can't render without conversion).

Left out at this depth: moderation/content scanning, CDN delivery configuration, and multi-photo reorder/delete UX — each a level down from the upload path itself.

Two places drive this: the pseudocode's inline `alert("quota exceeded", tenant)` after each `govern()` call, and the eight-condition list in Observability.

The fork that matters: those eight conditions aren't all the same shape.

- **Four are direct guardrail fires** — `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`. These read straight off `result.guardrail` each cycle, same as the pseudocode already does. Trivial to extend.
- **Three need cross-cycle counting** — `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned two cycles running, pace error over 15% two cycles running. `govern()` is stateless per the Core purity section, so these counters can't live inside it without polluting the thing the simulation harness stress-tests. Keep them in a small supervisor-side alerting record, separate from the persisted controller state, updated from each `result` after the pure call returns.
- **Heartbeat-missed is the odd one out** — nothing inside a cycle can raise it, because the failure mode is the cycle not running at all. That has to be an external dead-man's switch: each successful sweep pings a heartbeat check, and an independent watchdog (Prometheus rule, Healthchecks.io, cron monitor) pages if no ping arrives within, say, two cycle-lengths. It can't be the supervisor alerting on itself.

One more decision worth calling out: several of these conditions *persist* (quota-zero holds till day-roll, floor_unreachable holds till fixed). Paging every 5 minutes while a state persists is noisy — fire on the transition into/out of the condition, not on every cycle it's still true. That's another reason the alerting record needs previous-vs-current, not just current.

Left out: actual alert-channel wiring (PagerDuty vs Slack vs email) and the specific thresholds/debounce windows — those are config, not architecture.

Given the shape of this service, there's one clean lever to build this on: `db.write()` in `db.js` is already the single chokepoint for every write, and it already wraps each one in `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`. That means you can get atomic, un-bypassable audit logging almost for free — a write and its audit record either both land or both roll back.

**Design: Postgres triggers + a per-transaction actor variable, not per-route logging.**

1. **Thread the actor through `write()`.** Change its signature to `write(text, params, actor)` where `actor` is `req.user` (or an explicit `{ id: 'system', email: 'system' }` for migrations/jobs — never leave it null, or you'll have unattributable rows). Inside the existing transaction, before the real query, run:
   ```sql
   SELECT set_config('app.actor_id', $1, true);
   SELECT set_config('app.actor_email', $2, true);
   ```
   `true` scopes it to the transaction, so it's gone after COMMIT/ROLLBACK and never leaks across pooled connections.

2. **One generic trigger, not app-side diffing.** Attach an `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger to each audited table (`accounts`, `orders`, etc.) that inserts into `audit_log(table_name, row_id, action, actor_id, actor_email, changed_at, old_row, new_row)` using `to_jsonb(OLD)`/`to_jsonb(NEW)` and `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)`. This is the key fork: doing it in the DB instead of in each route means a new route or a future column added to `orders` is captured automatically — nobody has to remember to call an audit helper. Route-level logging (e.g., building the audit row by hand in `accounts.js`/`orders.js`) is more readable but silently rots the moment someone adds a write and forgets it.

3. **Lock the audit table down**: app's DB role gets `INSERT` only on `audit_log`, no `UPDATE`/`DELETE`, ideally owned by a different role than the app uses. That's the practical bar for "compliance-grade" — a compromised app credential or a rogue admin using the app can't rewrite history. If the compliance requirement goes further (regulator audits, SOC2 with a stricter tamper-evidence bar), stream `audit_log` out via logical replication to an external append-only sink (S3 with Object Lock is the common choice) so a DB-admin-level compromise still leaves an untouched copy elsewhere — but I'd only build that if it's actually asked for, since it's a real infra lift.

One gap worth flagging since it undercuts "who" specifically: `accounts.js` (`PATCH/DELETE /:id`) and `orders.js` (`PATCH /:id/cancel`) never check that `req.params.id` belongs to `req.user.accountId` — any authenticated user can write to any account/order. The audit trail will faithfully record which authenticated user did it, but won't tell you whether they were supposed to be able to.

Cache the query results, not the whole page — product data is mostly shared across users; only things like personalized pricing or live inventory counts aren't cacheable the same way.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Invalidation** — TTL (e.g., 30–60s, simple, some staleness) vs. event-driven (invalidate/refresh on product write, fresher but needs a hook into wherever products get updated). If writes are rare and reads are massive (typical for a catalog), event-driven pays for itself.
2. **Where it lives** — in-process/local cache (fastest, but goes stale across instances, needs a short TTL as a backstop) vs. a shared store like Redis (consistent across instances, one extra network hop, easy to invalidate from a single place).

Recommendation: Redis keyed by product ID, read-through (miss → hit DB → populate), invalidated on write in the product-update path. That gets you off the 900ms without relying on a timer to paper over staleness.

Left out of this sketch: stampede protection when a hot key expires under concurrent load, and whether any per-user fields force a partial cache/partial-live split on the page.

Enforce it at the API gateway/edge, not deep in application code, using a per-client token bucket keyed by API key or client ID (not IP — one client can span many IPs, or many clients can share one). Back the bucket with Redis (atomic INCR+TTL or a Lua script) so all gateway instances share state. On limit breach, return `429` with a `Retry-After` header, and expose `X-RateLimit-Limit`/`-Remaining` so well-behaved clients can self-throttle.

Two decisions actually fork this design:

1. **Where enforcement happens** — at the gateway, the noisy client gets rejected before touching your backend/DB, which is what fixes "degrading it for everybody else." In app middleware, the request still consumes backend resources before being turned away, which doesn't solve your actual problem.
2. **Flat cap vs. adaptive limits** — a flat per-client rate (e.g. N req/s with some burst allowance) is enough for a single misbehaving client. Adaptive limits (tightening caps as backend load rises) matter if legitimate traffic is bursty and you don't want to punish it at a fixed threshold.

Left out at this altitude: exact bucket-size/refill-rate tuning, race conditions in the distributed counter under very high QPS, and alerting on who's repeatedly hitting the ceiling.

Recommendation: server-sent events (SSE), not polling. Ops dashboards are one-directional (server → client), and SSE gives you push updates over plain HTTP with automatic reconnection built into the browser's `EventSource` API — no need for full WebSocket complexity.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Push vs. poll** — SSE only works well if your backend can hold long-lived connections. If it's serverless/behind a proxy that kills long requests, fall back to polling every few seconds with a stale-while-revalidate pattern so the UI still feels live.
2. **Data source shape** — if dashboard changes are driven by discrete events (a job finishes, an alert fires), wire the SSE stream to that event bus/queue so updates push the instant they happen. If it's aggregated metrics recomputed on a schedule, there's nothing to "push" faster than the recompute interval, so a timer-driven refresh is just as fresh and much simpler.

Left out: scaling SSE/WebSocket connections across multiple backend instances needs a fan-out layer (Redis pub/sub or similar) so an event on one server reaches clients connected to another.

The core fix isn't "retry the charge" — it's don't let a timeout mean "failed." A gateway timeout tells you nothing about whether the charge actually went through; retrying blindly risks double-charging, and showing "payment failed" when it might have succeeded is the actual customer-facing bug.

Shape it as three pieces:
1. **Idempotency key per checkout attempt** (not per HTTP request), stored with the order and passed to the processor on every retry — this is what makes retrying safe at all.
2. **On timeout, check status before acting.** Query the processor for that idempotency key/charge reference first; only retry if it's genuinely unresolved.
3. **Order status becomes an explicit state machine** (pending → processing → succeeded/failed), driven by that record rather than the original request — so the customer sees "processing," not "failed," until you have a real answer, and retries survive if the original request thread dies.

The one decision that actually forks the design: **inline retry vs. async.** At "a few times a day" volume, retrying synchronously with backoff for a few seconds before responding is simplest and probably enough. If the processor call itself can hang rather than fail fast, you want async instead — return "processing" immediately, resolve via webhook/job, and push the final status to the client.

What stack/processor are you on (Stripe, Adyen, in-house)? That decides whether idempotency keys and status lookups are handled for you or need to be built.

Start with Postgres full-text search — a `tsvector` column combining name (weighted A) and description (weighted B), a GIN index, and `ts_rank` for ordering — rather than standing up a dedicated search service. It handles typical catalog sizes, needs no new infra, and stays transactionally consistent with the products table.

Two decisions actually fork this:

- **Scale/features vs. simplicity**: if the catalog is large (millions of rows) or you'll need typo-tolerance, faceted filtering, or sub-50ms latency, move to a dedicated engine (Typesense or Meilisearch for simplicity, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need it elsewhere too). That means running and syncing a second data store — real operational cost, so don't default to it.
- **Sync strategy**: a trigger or application-level write updating the `tsvector` column keeps things simple for Postgres search; a separate search engine instead needs an event/queue-driven reindex path, which is where most of the complexity in that option actually lives.

Left out at this level: tokenization/stemming config, synonym handling, and how "matching by name and description" gets weighted against each other in ranking — worth a follow-up once the backend choice is made.

Have the client request a presigned upload URL from your backend, then PUT the photo directly to object storage (S3/R2/GCS) — don't proxy multi-MB phone photos through your app server. Before that PUT, resize/recompress client-side (canvas, cap the long edge around 2000–2500px, JPEG quality ~80, convert HEIC to JPEG for iOS Safari) so you're not shipping 8–12MB originals over cellular. Once the object lands, a storage-triggered function generates thumbnail and display-size variants, and the listing shows the photo as "processing" until that write completes.

Two decisions actually fork this build: direct-to-storage (presigned URL) vs. proxying uploads through your app, and client-side vs. server-side resize/compression. Direct-to-storage plus client-side downscale is the standard pattern at phone-photo volumes. The depth I'm skipping: resumable/chunked upload for flaky mobile connections — worth adding if sellers are uploading on spotty cell signal.

Two things make this harder than "call `alert()` where the pseudocode shows it":

**The pseudocode's alert call is a placeholder, not the real design.** `govern()` is pure and owns guardrail decisions; guardrails are evaluated in priority order with only one winner per cycle. But the alert list (SPEC.md:64-73) includes conditions that never correspond to a guardrail at all — heartbeat missed, cap pinned for two consecutive cycles, pace error above 15% for two consecutive cycles. If `quota_exceeded` wins the priority race in a given cycle, a simultaneous `floor_at_risk` condition is real but invisible to the single `result.guardrail` field. So alerting can't just watch which guardrail fired; it needs its own evaluator that inspects the underlying state/inputs independently of priority-order masking, run by the supervisor right after `persist_state`, alongside (not inside) the `govern()` call.

**Heartbeat-missed can't be detected from inside the loop.** By definition, if the loop didn't run, no code path executed to notice. That alert has to come from something external — a watchdog that checks "has tenant X persisted a cycle in the last N minutes?" against the persisted state's timestamp, on its own schedule.

The two consecutive-cycle conditions (cap pinned, pace error) need short history, not just current state — either extend the persisted controller state with a small rolling window, or have the supervisor keep last-cycle results in memory and compare.

Left out: alert delivery/dedup (rate-limiting repeat fires, routing by severity) and where thresholds like "15%" and "two/three cycles" live in config — SPEC.md doesn't say.

Every write in this service already funnels through one place — `db.write()` in `db.js` — so that's the interception point, but I'd enforce the audit trail one layer below it, in Postgres, not in that function itself.

**Recommendation:** row-level triggers on each mutable table (`accounts`, `orders`, ...) that insert into an append-only `audit_log` table on `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`, capturing `OLD`/`NEW` as jsonb. Triggers can't be skipped by a route that forgets to log, or by a future write path that bypasses `db.write()` entirely — which matters for compliance, since the failure mode you're guarding against is someone adding a write six months from now and not knowing an audit hook exists.

The one gap triggers have: they see the row change but not *who* asked for it. Close that with a single addition to `db.write()` — right after `BEGIN`, run `SET LOCAL audit.actor = $1` with `req.user.id` (currently `req.user` is only in Express's `req`, so `write()` needs that id passed in or read from an async-local-storage context set by `sessionUser`). The trigger reads it back with `current_setting('audit.actor', true)` and stamps it on the row it inserts. Same transaction, so actor and change are atomic — no window where a write commits without its attribution.

Lock the table down after that: revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on `audit_log` from the app's DB role, grant it only `INSERT`. That's what makes it an audit trail rather than a log someone can quietly edit.

Left at the next level down: the exact `audit_log` schema (table, row id, action, actor, old/new, timestamp, and whether you want a request id for grouping multi-row writes into one logical change), and how compliance actually queries it — a read-only view, an export job, or a separate reporting store if they need it retained longer than the primary DB.

Cache-aside with Redis at the query-result level (product row, price, inventory — not full rendered HTML), keyed by product ID, TTL of a few minutes as backstop plus explicit invalidation on writes (product/price/inventory updates publish a cache-bust for that key). Add jitter or a lock/single-flight on cache miss so a popular product doesn't trigger a stampede of concurrent DB hits when it expires.

Two things that actually fork the design, depending on what's not shown here:
- **Granularity** — full-page caching is fastest but breaks the moment there's personalization, A/B tests, or per-user pricing; query-level composes fine with dynamic bits and is the safer default unless the page is fully static per product.
- **Invalidation** — TTL-only is simplest to build but means edits can show stale data for up to the TTL window; event-driven invalidation is correct but requires touching every write path that changes product data.

What's the stack (which DB, and is there already a cache/queue in place)? That decides whether event-driven invalidation is cheap to wire up or a bigger lift.

Reading `routes/api.js`: the auth middleware already resolves every request to `req.client.client_id` and `req.client.plan` before it hits a route handler. That's the key, not IP — the code even calls out that clients share NATs and span multiple addresses, so IP-based limiting would both over- and under-block.

Two decisions actually fork this:

**Key by `client_id`, not IP.** Add a second middleware in `routes/api.js` right after the auth one, since that's the first point `req.client` exists. Bonus: `req.client.plan` gives you per-plan limits for free without a new lookup.

**State has to live in Redis, not memory.** `app.js` forks 4 workers per box behind a load balancer with nothing shared in module scope — an in-process counter would let each client burst 4x (or more, across boxes) before any single worker noticed. `redis.js` already gives you a shared client every worker talks to, so put the counter there: a fixed-window `INCR` + `EXPIRE` on `rl:{client_id}:{window}` is enough, or a Lua script if you want sliding-window accuracy and want to avoid the race between `INCR` and `EXPIRE` on key creation. On limit exceeded, `res.status(429)` with `Retry-After` before the Postgres query runs, so the offending client's load never reaches the database — the actual resource the "degrading it for everybody else" is about.

Left out: choice of algorithm (fixed window vs. sliding-window log vs. token bucket) and the actual per-plan numbers — that's a tuning pass once you see the offending client's real traffic shape.

Poll, not push — the platform rules out anything else. `PLATFORM.md` says WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, functions die at 10s, and there's no sticky routing or shared memory, so SSE/long-polling can't be held open or fanned out either. Only client-initiated polling works.

Since `jobs/rollup.md` says the rollup table changes exactly once a minute, on the minute, dumb interval polling would mean most requests return unchanged data. Better: poll on a schedule anchored to that cadence. In `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click-only `load()` with a loop that fetches `/api/metrics`, compares the new `computed_at` to the last-seen value, re-renders only on change, and schedules the next poll for shortly after the next minute boundary (falling back to a short fixed interval if a poll fails, so it self-heals if it ever drifts). `api/metrics.js` needs no change — it's already a cheap 30ms/4KB read with `no-store`.

Left out: backoff/error handling on fetch failure, and pausing the poll loop via the Page Visibility API when the tab isn't focused.

The core issue: a timeout isn't a failure, it's an *unknown* — the charge may have actually gone through on the processor's side. Retrying without accounting for that is how customers get double-charged.

Recommended shape:
- Generate one idempotency key per logical charge attempt (not per HTTP retry) and pass it to the processor on every retry of that same charge. Stripe/Adyen/etc. all support this — it makes a duplicate request a no-op instead of a second charge.
- Persist charge state server-side as pending → processing → succeeded/failed/unknown, rather than deriving status from a single request/response. On timeout, land in `unknown`, not `failed`.
- Before retrying, query the processor for the charge's actual status using that idempotency key. Only retry if it's genuinely not there; otherwise reconcile to `succeeded`.
- Retry with backoff (e.g. 3 attempts, exponential + jitter) in a background job, not inline in the request — the client may have already given up waiting.
- Customer sees "processing"/"confirming payment" during this window, not "payment failed".

The one decision that really forks the design: **synchronous inline retry vs. async job + reconciliation.** Inline is simpler but still leaves the client hanging on a slow processor and can't do a clean pre-retry status check. Async is more robust (survives the client disconnecting, handles the query-before-retry safely) but needs a job queue, persisted charge state, and a way to push the resolved status back to the UI (poll or webhook-driven update).

Left out here: what happens after max retries are exhausted (dead-letter to manual review vs. auto-fail), and webhook-driven reconciliation for charges that succeed *after* you've stopped retrying. Worth designing once I know which payment processor and stack you're on.

For a few-word query matching against name/description, that's classic full-text search: tokenize and index both fields, query with ranking (prefix matching helps for partial typing), return top-N sorted by relevance.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Engine.** If the catalog is small-to-medium (up to ~100k products) and you're already on Postgres, its built-in full-text search (`tsvector`/`tsquery` with a GIN index) is enough and avoids a new service. Past that scale, or if you want typo-tolerance/faster iteration on ranking, a dedicated search engine (Typesense, Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) is worth the added ops.

2. **Freshness.** Products change (price, stock, description edits) — you need the index kept in sync with the source of truth, either via a write-path hook/trigger that updates the index on every product write, or a periodic batch reindex if near-real-time isn't required.

Left out: ranking tuning (boosting name matches over description matches, handling typos/synonyms) and query-side UX (debouncing, autocomplete) — those are refinements once the base index is in place, not fork points.

Direct-to-bucket upload, not through the app server: have the client PUT straight to S3 using a presigned URL, the same mechanism `storage.signedUrl` already supports for reads (it's currently only used for the invoice GET, but the `PUT` branch and the bucket's CORS rule for `market.example.com` are already there, unused).

That's forced by nginx.conf: `client_max_body_size 1m` is set globally on the listener that also fronts payments, and a per-location override was explicitly declined for PCI reasons. A phone camera photo is routinely 3-12MB, so proxying the upload through `market.example.com` the way `/pay/` and `/admin` are proxied isn't an option — the bytes have to skip that listener entirely, which is exactly what a presigned PUT to the bucket does.

Concretely:
- New route mirrors `GET /:id/invoice`: something like `POST /:id/photos` looks up the listing, builds a key (`listings/${id}/${uuid}.jpg`), and returns `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT' })`.
- Client resizes/re-encodes the photo before sending it (canvas downscale to a couple thousand px on the long edge, JPEG quality ~0.8) — this has to happen client-side, not server-side, since the bytes never pass through your server at all.
- Client PUTs the compressed file directly to the signed URL, then calls back to your API to confirm success, which runs `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)`.

One thing this doesn't give you: server-verified size/content-type limits, since a bare presigned PUT trusts the client. If sellers' phones turning out to send unreasonably large or wrong-type files becomes a real problem, the fallback is presigned POST with policy conditions (content-length-range, content-type) instead of PUT — more setup than what's already wired up, so I'd only reach for it if compression alone proves unreliable. Thumbnail/variant generation for listing display is also out of scope of the upload path itself — that'd be a separate async job triggered off the bucket's ObjectCreated event.

Two things fire alerts here, and they don't have the same shape.

Seven of the eight conditions are things `govern()` can already see or nearly see — `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`, and `feed_stale`-past-three are guardrail outputs; the two "N consecutive cycles" conditions (cap pinned, pace error >15%) need a streak counter the same way `feed_stale` already tracks "three consecutive" in persisted state. So extend `govern()`'s return from a single winning guardrail to a small structured set of alert flags (it stays pure — the counters live in the state that's already threaded in and out), and turn the supervisor's one-line `if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded"` into a lookup over that set.

The eighth — heartbeat missed — can't come from `govern()` at all, since it's defined by the loop *not* running. That has to be an external watchdog: something outside the per-tenant cycle that checks each tenant's last-recorded-cycle timestamp against the 5-minute cadence and alerts on staleness (a dead-man's-switch, e.g. cron-based check or monitoring-system heartbeat metric).

Left out at this level: the actual alert transport/dedup (paging vs. log vs. Slack, and whether repeated cycles re-alert or suppress) — that's a routing detail, not a fork in the core design.

Looked at the service: `db.js` already funnels every write through one `write()` function that wraps BEGIN/COMMIT, and `auth.js` sets `req.user` (id, email, accountId) on every request before it reaches a route. That's the natural seam.

**Recommendation:** log audit rows from inside `write()`, in the same transaction as the change, not from each route handler. Concretely: add an `audit_log` table (actor_id, actor_email, table/action or the raw SQL + params, before/after if you can get it via `RETURNING`, timestamp, request id) and have `write()` insert into it right after the query, before COMMIT — so an audit entry and the change it describes commit or roll back together, and no route can forget to log. Grant the app's DB role INSERT-only on that table (no UPDATE/DELETE) so it's append-only for compliance purposes.

**The one thing that forks this:** `write()` doesn't currently know who's calling — `req.user` lives in Express middleware, not in `db.js`. Two ways to get it there: thread the actor as an explicit argument through every `write()` call site (touches every route file, but is grep-able and obvious), or set it once via `AsyncLocalStorage` in `sessionUser` and have `write()` read it implicitly (no call-site changes, but the actor is "ambient" and easy to lose track of).
