Upload photos straight to S3 with a presigned PUT, not through the app/nginx — `storage.js:10-16` already supports `method: 'PUT'` and the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com`; it's just never been called with that option. That's forced by `nginx.conf`: `client_max_body_size 1m` is global across the storefront/payments/admin listener and was deliberately kept unraised and non-overridable for PCI reasons, and a phone photo is routinely 3-8MB, so proxying the bytes through the app server isn't an option here.

Flow: `routes/listings.js` gets a new `POST /:id/photos` that generates a key and returns `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT' })` (a small JSON round-trip, well under the 1m cap) — the browser PUTs the image bytes directly to S3, bypassing nginx entirely — then a follow-up call (or the same request, once the PUT succeeds) does `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` to append into `listing.photo_keys`.

The part worth deciding next: whether the server trusts the client's "upload succeeded" callback to record the key, or verifies the object exists in S3 first (HEAD request) before writing to `photo_keys` — that's a fraud/race-condition tradeoff, not an architecture one.

Two categories, and they don't belong in the same mechanism:

**The four single-cycle guardrails** (`quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`) are just `result.guardrail` values already returned by `govern()`. The supervisor checks the result after step 4 and fires directly — same place `alert("quota exceeded", tenant)` already sits in the pseudocode, extended to the other three.

**The three streak conditions** (`feed_stale` × 3, cap pinned × 2, pace error > 15% × 2) need consecutive-cycle memory. That memory shouldn't live inside `govern()`'s persisted state — the core-purity section is explicit that `govern()` is pure and the test/simulation ladder depends on that; alert bookkeeping is I/O and has no bearing on the cap decision. So it's a second, separate piece of per-tenant state the supervisor reads/writes right alongside `persist_state`, incrementing on match and resetting on break, firing when the streak hits threshold.

**Heartbeat missed is the odd one out** — it can't be detected by code inside the loop, because a missed run means no code executes at all. That needs an external dead-man's-switch: each completed cycle pings a timestamp somewhere outside the tenant loop (a metrics push, a healthcheck ping), and a separate watchdog alerts if that timestamp goes stale past one cycle interval.

So three mechanisms, not one: inline check on `govern()`'s return value, a small streak counter next to (but not inside) the persisted controller state, and an external heartbeat watchdog. The one real design decision underneath this is where the streak counters get persisted — in-memory per supervisor process is fine if the supervisor is a long-lived singleton per tenant; if it's not (restarts, multiple workers), they need to move into the same durable store as `result.state`, just in a field `govern()` never reads.

Good news for this: every write already funnels through one place — `db.write()` in db.js:13, and `req.user` is resolved before every route handler by the `sessionUser` middleware in auth.js. That's the natural hook point; you don't need to touch the route handlers in accounts.js/orders.js at all.

Recommendation: add a Postgres audit table + trigger, not application-level logging scattered in `write()`. Two forking decisions:

- **Where "who" comes from**: `db.write()` doesn't currently receive `req.user`, and a DB trigger can't see it either. Have `write()` run `SET LOCAL app.user_id = $1` (from the caller's `req.user.id`) as the first statement in its existing transaction, then have an `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` trigger on each audited table read that session variable via `current_setting('app.user_id', true)` into the audit row. This keeps "who" flowing through the one chokepoint you already have, without threading it through every call site.
- **App-level hook vs. DB trigger**: logging inside `write()` is less work now but only catches writes that go through the app — it'd miss migrations, admin scripts, or any future direct-SQL path. A trigger catches every write regardless of source and can't be bypassed by a route that forgets to log, at the cost of needing the session-variable plumbing above to still capture "who."

Audit row shape: table, row id, action, `old_row`/`new_row` as `jsonb` (trigger has both via `OLD`/`NEW`), user id, timestamp — written in the same transaction as the write itself, so it's atomic with it and rolls back together on failure.

Left out: retention/immutability policy (e.g. revoke UPDATE/DELETE on the audit table itself, or ship it to WORM storage) and whether reads also need auditing — worth a separate pass once the write trail is in place.

Cache-aside with Redis in front of the DB query (or the fully rendered page fragment), keyed by product ID, with a short TTL (minutes) as a safety net plus explicit invalidation fired from the product-update/price/stock-change write path. That turns the 900ms DB round-trip into a ~5ms cache hit on almost every request, since product pages are read-heavy and the underlying data changes rarely relative to traffic.

Two things actually fork the design:

- **Granularity**: cache the raw DB query result vs. the rendered HTML/JSON page. Raw-query caching is safer if any part of the page is personalized (per-user pricing, "in your cart," locale); full-page caching is faster but breaks the moment personalization creeps in. Given you said "nearly all of it is the database," cache at the query/data layer, not the rendered page — cheaper to invalidate correctly and doesn't foreclose personalization later.
- **Invalidation trigger**: TTL-only is simplest but means stale prices/stock for up to the TTL window; event-driven invalidation (bust the key when the product write happens) is what you actually want for price/stock-sensitive fields, with TTL kept only as a fallback for missed invalidations.

Add single-flight/request-coalescing on cache miss (a lock or "in-flight" marker per key) so a popular product's cache expiry doesn't send a thundering herd of concurrent requests to the DB at once — that's the failure mode that bites teams after this exact fix.

Key on `req.client.client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware in `routes/api.js:9-19` already resolves that before any handler runs, and the comment above it flags that multiple clients share addresses behind NAT, so IP-based limiting would throttle innocent neighbors instead of the offender.

Enforce it in Redis, not in-process: `app.js` forks 4 workers per box with no shared memory, and Redis (`redis.js`) is already the one store all workers and boxes share, so it's the only place a counter is consistent across the fleet. Add a middleware right after the auth block that does an atomic `INCR`+`EXPIRE` (or a small Lua script for atomicity) on a key like `rl:{client_id}:{windowStart}`, checks it against a per-plan limit (plan is already sitting on `req.client`), and returns 429 with `Retry-After` before the request reaches the DB.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:
- **Algorithm**: fixed-window counter (one INCR+EXPIRE, cheapest) vs. sliding-window/token-bucket (smoother, no boundary burst, costs a Lua script or sorted set). Fixed-window is enough unless the "hammering" pattern is bursty right at window edges.
- **Fail-open vs fail-closed on Redis errors**: since Redis is a hard dependency for sessions already, fail-closed (reject) is consistent with existing behavior, but worth confirming that's acceptable if Redis blips.

Left out: exact limit numbers per plan, and whether to layer a cheap per-IP cap in front as DoS protection in addition to the per-client one.

Replace `dashboard.js`'s click-driven `load()` with a `setInterval` poll of `/api/metrics`, re-rendering only when `computed_at` changes.

That's the only option here, not one of several: the platform doc rules out WebSockets and SSE outright (connection upgrades 501 at the edge, functions frozen between invocations, no sticky routing to keep a subscription alive). Polling is what's left.

The one real decision is the interval. `rollup` is rewritten once a minute by a fixed job — polling faster than that just burns serverless invocations for identical rows. Poll every 60s, and skip the re-render when `computed_at` matches the last value you saw (cheap since the row already carries that timestamp, avoids flicker on ties). Pausing the interval on `document.visibilitychange` when the tab isn't visible is worth adding too, given each poll is a billed invocation.

Left out: retry/backoff behavior if a poll fails, and whether to stagger poll start times across clients so they aren't all hitting the function in the same instant right after the minute rolls over.

The fix is idempotency, not just retrying — a timeout means you don't know if the charge landed on the processor's side, so blindly retrying risks double-charging the customer.

**Core design:**
1. Generate one idempotency key per payment attempt and reuse it across retries. Every major processor (Stripe, Braintree, Adyen) dedupes on that key, so retrying with the same key is safe even if the original request actually succeeded.
2. Classify the failure before deciding to retry: timeouts/5xx/network errors are retryable; declines/insufficient funds/card errors are not — those should still surface as real failures immediately.
3. Don't retry synchronously in the request that's already timing out. Mark the attempt "pending," persist it, and either look up the actual charge status by idempotency key or enqueue a background retry with backoff (e.g. 3 attempts, 2s/10s/60s).
4. Drive retries off stored state — a `charge_attempts` table (idempotency_key, status, attempt_count, last_error) — not off the client re-submitting.
5. Customer sees "processing," not "failed," while retries are in flight; "failed" only shows after retries exhaust or a genuine decline comes back.

Left out: webhook-based reconciliation for attempts that resolve after your process moves on, and making the retry queue durable across restarts. Which processor are you on — that determines the exact idempotency/lookup API to use.

Direct-to-S3 via presigned PUT, bypassing nginx entirely for the actual bytes:

1. Client asks the app server for a presigned PUT URL (tiny JSON request, well under any body cap).
2. Server calls `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT' })` — already supported, unused today (storage.js:11-16).
3. Phone uploads the photo straight to S3 with that URL.
4. Client reports success back to the server, which calls `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` (db.js:10-12) to append to `photo_keys`.

The fork that decides this: nginx's `client_max_body_size 1m` (nginx.conf:12) is shared across the storefront, payments, and admin listeners, and raising it — even per-location — was explicitly declined for PCI reasons. A phone photo routinely exceeds 1MB, so proxying the bytes through the app server is off the table; presigned PUT is the only path that doesn't touch that limit, and the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com` (storage.js:12-13) for exactly this.

Left for the next level down: client-side resize/compression before upload (nice for phone camera files, not required since S3 has no comparable size cap), and how `addPhotoKey` handles a client that never reports back (orphaned S3 object, no DB row).

Two things fork the design, both visible in the doc itself.

**Where "N consecutive cycles" logic lives.** `govern()` is documented as pure (SPEC.md:37-42) and only returns a single `guardrail` for the current cycle — it has no memory of prior cycles' guardrails, cap-clamp status, or pace error. But three of the eight alert conditions (SPEC.md:66-73) are multi-cycle: `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned two cycles, pace error >15% for two cycles. You have two options: hand-roll consecutive-count counters in the supervisor's persisted state, or have the supervisor emit one structured event per tenant per cycle (guardrail, cap, pace error, band-edge flag) to a metrics pipeline and define the "N consecutive" conditions as alert rules there (e.g. Prometheus `for:` clauses). I'd push it to the metrics backend — it's the standard tool for this exact shape and keeps `govern()`'s test ladder (SPEC.md:38-42) untouched, versus growing bespoke counters that need their own tests and get persisted alongside controller state.

**Heartbeat-missed can't be emitted by the loop.** Every other alert condition is something the loop notices and reports; "the loop did not run" (SPEC.md:66) is the loop's absence, so the loop itself can't be the thing that raises it. That needs an external dead-man's-switch — something outside the supervisor expecting a per-tenant heartbeat/metric every 5 minutes and alerting when one doesn't arrive.

Left for the next level down: which metrics/alerting system to wire into (depends on what's already in the stack), and the exact alert routing/severity mapping for each of the eight conditions.

Every write in this service already funnels through one place — `db.write()` in `db.js` — and every request already resolves `req.user` before hitting a route. That choke point is the natural hook, but it exposes the real gap: `write()` takes only `(text, params)`, so it has no idea who's calling right now.

**Recommended shape:** capture audit rows with a Postgres trigger on each audited table (`accounts`, `orders`, ...), not application code. A row-level `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger writes `table, row_id, op, old_row jsonb, new_row jsonb, txid, changed_at` into an insert-only `audit_log` table, inside the same transaction as the write — so it's atomic with the change and catches anything that touches the table, including a future route someone adds without thinking about audit, or a one-off fix run from `psql`.

**The fork that matters here:** a trigger only sees the DB role, not `req.user`. To get "who" into it, `db.write()` needs to run `SET LOCAL app.user_id = $1` at the top of its existing `BEGIN`, and the trigger reads it back with `current_setting('app.user_id', true)`. That means threading the acting user into `write()` — either add it as an explicit third argument and update the three call sites in `routes/`, or set it implicitly via `AsyncLocalStorage` populated once in `sessionUser` (auth.js:5) so `write()` reads it without touching every call site. I'd pick the explicit-argument version: implicit context is convenient but makes it easy for a write to silently log `NULL` as the actor if it happens outside a request (a script, a migration), and compliance is exactly the case where a silent gap is the failure mode you can't afford.

Depth I'm leaving out: retention/immutability of `audit_log` itself (revoke UPDATE/DELETE from the app role, maybe ship rows to WORM storage), and whether reads need auditing too (you asked about writes, so I stuck to that).

Cache `/p` at the edge — the CDN's already in front of every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the app sends; the reason it's at 0% hit rate is `middleware/security.js` sending blanket `no-store` app-wide. Two decisions:

**Scope the no-store override, don't remove it.** That header exists because an account page once leaked through an intermediary cache, and `/account` genuinely needs it (per-user, reads `req.session.userId`). `/p/:slug` is different: no session read, identical for every visitor. In `routes/products.js`, overwrite `Cache-Control` after the security middleware runs — Express lets a later handler replace headers before the response is sent — with something like `public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300`. Policy stays in the app, in one place, matching the contract in `CDN.md`; `/account` is untouched.

**Pick the TTL around the piece that goes stale fastest.** The 900ms is `productBySlug` (~40ms) + `relatedProducts`' four-table join (~600ms) + `stockFor` (~250ms). Catalog edits land a few times a day, but stock moves on every purchase, so any public cache risks showing stale stock for the TTL window. A 60s `max-age` with a 300s `stale-while-revalidate` bounds that to about a minute, and lets the first stale hit trigger a background refetch instead of making the user wait — origin DB load drops from every request to roughly once per product per minute.

Left unexplored: if sub-minute stock accuracy actually matters commercially, split the page into a long-TTL cached shell (product + related) and a separate, much-shorter-TTL stock fetch — more moving parts, only worth it if staleness on stock specifically is a real business problem.

Identify the offending client by API key (or client ID), not just IP — since IP alone won't distinguish a legit multi-user proxy from a single bad actor — and enforce a token-bucket limit per client at the edge (gateway/middleware), before requests reach the `/v1` handler, returning `429` with `Retry-After` once they're over quota.

The one decision that really forks this: single instance vs. horizontally scaled. Single instance, an in-memory counter per client is enough. Multiple instances, counters need to live in something shared and fast (Redis is the standard choice) or each instance's independent limit lets the client burst past the intended total by hitting different instances.

Left out: tuning burst size vs. sustained rate, and whether to give different tiers different limits (paying vs. free clients) — that's policy, not mechanism, and worth deciding after you see this client's actual traffic shape.

Two ways to do this, and the choice mostly comes down to how fresh the data needs to be:

**Polling** — client re-fetches on an interval (`setInterval` + fetch, or a library like SWR/React Query with `refetchInterval`). Simple, works with any backend, no new infrastructure. Fine if a 10-30s staleness window is acceptable.

**Push** (SSE or WebSocket) — server notifies the client when data changes. Needed if updates must appear within a second or two, or if polling load becomes a problem at scale. SSE is the simpler of the two (one-directional, plain HTTP, auto-reconnect) and is usually the better fit for a dashboard that only needs to receive updates, not send them.

Recommendation: start with polling unless you already know sub-second freshness matters — it's a few lines of code and no new moving parts. Move to SSE only if polling proves too slow or too chatty.

What I'm leaving out: how the backend detects "something changed" to push (DB triggers, change-data-capture, a message queue) — that's the real complexity if you go the push route, and it depends on what's producing the dashboard's data.

The critical thing: a timeout doesn't mean the charge failed — it means you don't know what happened. The request may have reached the processor and succeeded, with only the response lost in transit. Retry logic that ignores this will occasionally double-charge people. So the design has three parts, in this order of importance:

**1. Idempotency keys, not blind retries.** Every charge attempt gets a unique key generated client- or server-side *before* the first attempt, and every retry reuses that same key. Processors like Stripe dedupe on it — if the original request actually succeeded, the retry returns the original result instead of creating a second charge. Without this, nothing else below is safe to do.

**2. Reconcile before you retry.** On timeout, don't immediately fire a second attempt. First ask the processor "what happened to request X?" (a status/lookup call, or Stripe's idempotent replay of the same request). Only fall through to a genuine retry if the answer is "we never got it" or "it's still pending" after a bounded wait. This turns "timeout" into one of: succeeded (just tell the customer), still processing (wait and re-check), or truly unsent (safe to retry).

**3. A state machine, not a boolean.** Charges need a status beyond succeeded/failed: `pending` → `unknown_awaiting_reconciliation` → `succeeded` / `failed`. A background job owns the `unknown` state, polls/retries with exponential backoff and jitter, caps attempts (e.g. 5 over ~10 min), and on exhaustion routes to manual review rather than silently failing.

**Customer-facing fix:** the "payment failed" message you're seeing today is almost certainly the timeout being caught and mapped straight to a failure state. Once step 3 exists, the UI should show "processing" during the unknown window and only render "failed" after reconciliation confirms an actual decline — that alone fixes the misleading message even before retries kick in.

The one thing worth deciding explicitly up front: how long the customer sits in "processing" before you either resolve it or give up and ask them to try again — that timeout budget is the main tuning knob for the whole system.

For a typical catalog, Postgres full-text search (`tsvector` over name + description, GIN index) is the pragmatic default — it's operationally free and fast enough into the millions of rows. The fork that actually matters: if you need typo-tolerance, prefix-as-you-type, or relevance tuning beyond ts_rank, that pushes you to a dedicated engine (Typesense/Meilisearch/Algolia) with its own sync pipeline — otherwise skip that complexity entirely.

The other real decision is indexing freshness: trigger-based tsvector updates on write keep it always current with zero extra infra, versus a dedicated engine needing a debounced reindex job on product changes.

Which one fits depends on catalog size and how much "did you mean" behavior you want — what's the rough product count?

**Recommendation: direct-to-object-storage upload via presigned URLs, with client-side resize before sending.**

Flow: client asks the backend for a presigned upload URL (auth'd, scoped to the listing), resizes/compresses the photo locally (cap ~2000px long edge, JPEG ~80% quality — turns a 8-12MB phone photo into a few hundred KB, and normalizes HEIC to JPEG), PUTs directly to S3/GCS/R2 using that URL, then tells the backend the object key so it can attach it to the listing and kick off async thumbnail generation + EXIF stripping (especially GPS, for seller privacy).

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Where resize happens** — client-side (cuts upload size/time on mobile networks, but needs per-platform image code) vs. server-side (simpler client, but your server eats full multi-MB raw uploads including HEIC).
- **Sync vs. async processing** — show the listing photo immediately from the original with thumbnails backfilled later, vs. block the UI until processing completes.

Left out: retry/resumability for flaky mobile connections, multi-photo batch/reorder UX, and cleanup of orphaned uploads that never got attached to a listing.

Two forks matter here, both visible from how `govern()` and the control loop are specified.

**1. Where the alert decision lives.** Most of the conditions in Observability are either a direct guardrail (`quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid` — trivial, mirror line 31-32) or a *consecutive-cycle* condition (`feed_stale` past 3 cycles, cap pinned for 2, pace error >15% for 2). Since core purity is the load-bearing property here (§ Core purity — the simulation harness replays at thousands of cycles/sec because `govern()` does no I/O), the consecutive counters belong in the persisted controller `state`, not in supervisor-side memory. Extend `state` with counters like `stale_cycles`, `pinned_cycles`, `pace_error_cycles`, have `govern()` update them and return an `alerts: []` list alongside `guardrail`, and let the supervisor just do `for a in result.alerts: alert(a, tenant)`. That keeps alert logic in the unit-test ladder and makes the shadow-week replay (§ Rollout) reproduce alert history too, not just caps.

**2. Heartbeat-missed can't come from `govern()`.** It's the absence of a cycle, and a function only executes when called — no code path inside the loop ever observes its own non-execution. That needs an external watchdog: something outside the 5-minute loop (a separate scheduled check, or a dead-man's-switch reading `persist_state`'s last-updated timestamp per tenant) that fires when a tenant's state hasn't been touched in >1 cycle interval.

One more decision worth pinning down before building: edge-triggered vs level-triggered. `quota_exceeded` holds the cap at zero for the rest of the day (§ Guardrails) — do you want one alert when it fires, or one every 5 minutes for hours? The spec's guardrail semantics ("first match wins", "holds it there") suggest edge-triggered (alert on transition into the condition), which the consecutive-counter approach above supports naturally if `alerts` only fires the tick the counter crosses its threshold.

Every write in this service already funnels through one place: `db.write()` in db.js, which explicitly owns the transaction boundary. That's the chokepoint to build on, but there's a gap — it takes `(text, params)` only, so it has no actor to attribute a write to. `req.user` never reaches it.

**Recommendation: capture the audit trail in Postgres via triggers, not in application code.**

- Add an append-only `audit_log` table (`table_name`, `row_pk`, `action`, `actor_id`, `changed_at`, `old_row jsonb`, `new_row jsonb`), with the app's DB role granted `INSERT` only — no `UPDATE`/`DELETE` — so the trail itself can't be edited or backdated, including by a future bug or a direct psql session.
- Put an `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger on each audited table (`accounts`, `orders`, ...) that writes the OLD/NEW diff automatically. This means the audit fires even for writes that don't go through `db.write` — a migration, a console fix, a future service — which an app-level log can never guarantee.
- Thread the actor through with `SET LOCAL app.user_id = $1` as the first statement inside `db.write`'s existing `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`, and have the trigger read it via `current_setting('app.user_id', true)`. That requires changing `write()`'s signature to accept the actor and updating every call site (accounts.js, orders.js) to pass `req.user.id` — the one real cost of this approach.

The fork is trigger-based (DB-level) vs. wrapping `db.write` to log from the app. App-level is easier to enrich with request context (route, IP) but only covers writes that go through that helper, and to know *what* changed you'd end up regex-parsing raw SQL text — fragile and exactly the kind of thing that quietly breaks compliance guarantees later. Trigger-based costs a schema migration and the call-site plumbing, but gives you completeness and tamper-resistance for free, which is what an audit trail is for.

Cache-aside with Redis: on a page load, check cache by key (product ID + locale/currency), miss falls to the DB and populates the cache; on product update, invalidate that key explicitly (via the write path or a change event) rather than relying only on a TTL. Keep a short TTL as a backstop for any invalidation gaps.

Two things that decide the shape:
- **What you cache** — raw query result vs. a fully rendered fragment. If nearly all of the 900ms is the DB (as you said), caching the query result/materialized product view is enough; you don't need to cache rendering.
- **Popular-product stampede** — many concurrent cache misses on the same key (e.g. after invalidation or on a hot item) can all hit the DB at once. Use request coalescing (single-flight) or stale-while-revalidate so one request repopulates the cache while others get the stale value.

What's the current stack — is Redis/Memcached already in place, or is that also up for choice?

Given the shape of this: clustered Express (4 workers/box, no shared memory) behind a load balancer, Redis already used as the one piece of shared state, and Postgres-backed API keys where `req.client.client_id` is known before the route runs.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

**Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The auth middleware comment already tells you why — one client hits from many addresses, and several clients share an address behind the same NAT. IP-based limiting would throttle innocent neighbors of the noisy client and let the noisy client dodge it by rotating source IPs. Key the limiter on `req.client.client_id`, set in `routes/api.js:12` right after the API-key lookup.

**Count in Redis, not in-process.** Workers don't share memory (`app.js`'s comment: "nothing in module scope is shared") and there are 4 workers × N boxes, so an in-memory counter only sees a fraction of a client's traffic. The core issue: a timeout doesn't mean the charge failed — it means you don't know what happened. Treating it as a definitive failure is what's producing the bad message and would also make a blind retry risk double-charging.

Build it as:

1. **Idempotency key per logical charge attempt**, generated client- or server-side before the first call, reused on every retry. Stripe/Adyen/etc. dedupe on this key, so a retry after a timeout either returns the original result or safely creates one charge — never two.
2. **Move the retry off the request path.** On timeout, record the charge as `pending` (not failed) and hand it to an async worker/queue with backoff (a few attempts over seconds-to-minutes). The customer-facing request returns immediately with a "processing" state instead of blocking or erroring.
3. **Resolve pending charges via the processor's source of truth** — a status lookup by idempotency key/charge ID, and/or the webhook event — rather than assuming the retry's own response is authoritative. Only mark `failed` once the processor confirms it, or retries are exhausted.
4. Customer sees "processing"/"confirming payment" while pending, and only sees "payment failed" once you actually know that.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

**Transport.** If updates are relatively infrequent (seconds, not sub-second) and mostly one-directional, use Server-Sent Events — it's plain HTTP, auto-reconnects, and needs no new infra. **How the backend learns data changed.** Either it already has a live source (DB change stream/CDC, message queue, existing event bus) it can forward to connected clients, or it doesn't and has to poll its own data sources on an interval and diff/broadcast changes to subscribers. The former is push all the way down and cheap; the latter is push-to-the-browser but poll-behind-the-scenes, which is often the pragmatic choice for dashboards backed by a plain database with no change feed.

Given that, the mainstream build is: backend polls or subscribes to its sources, computes what changed, and fans it out over SSE to connected dashboard clients, which patch the UI incrementally rather than reloading. 2. **Retry blind vs. query-first.** Before retrying, ask the processor for the charge's current status by idempotency key. This catches the "it actually succeeded" case immediately instead of firing a redundant attempt and waiting on a webhook to sort it out.

The real bug isn't the retry — it's that a timeout gets mapped to "payment failed" when it actually means "unknown state." Two things follow from that:

**Idempotency first.** Every charge attempt needs an idempotency key sent to the processor (Stripe/Adyen/etc. support this natively). Without it, retrying a timed-out charge risks double-charging the customer if the original actually went through.

**Reconcile before you retry.** On a timeout, don't blindly resubmit — look up the charge by idempotency key first. If the processor already has it (succeeded or failed), adopt that result. Only create a new attempt if it's genuinely missing. This is what makes retrying safe rather than just adding a second race.

The one decision that really forks the design: **sync inline retry vs. async resolve.** Synchronous (retry once or twice within the same request before responding) is simpler but keeps the customer's browser blocked on a processor that just proved it's slow or unreachable — compounding the problem. Async (return "processing," resolve via a background job or the processor's webhook, then notify the customer) handles that better and matches what a timeout is actually telling you, at the cost of needing a pending-state UI and a follow-up notification path. Given it's only a few times a day, I'd lean async.

Left out: the specific backoff/retry-count schedule and the idempotency-key storage/dedup-window details — those are the next layer down once the sync-vs-async call is made.

The core issue: a timeout is ambiguous, not a failure — you don't actually know if the charge landed. Retrying blindly risks double-charging; showing "failed" when it may have succeeded loses the sale or triggers a duplicate attempt from the customer.

Recommended approach:
1. Generate an idempotency key per logical charge attempt (order ID, not per HTTP call) and pass it to the processor on every attempt, including retries. Most processors (Stripe, etc.) dedupe on this key, so a retry that lands on top of a charge that actually succeeded returns the original result instead of charging again.
2. On timeout, don't retry immediately — query the processor for the charge's actual status first, then only retry if it's genuinely absent/failed.
3. Move this off the customer's request entirely: return "processing" (not "failed"), enqueue a background job to do the reconcile-then-retry, and notify the customer async (webhook to your backend, then email/push) once it resolves.

The fork that matters: synchronous inline retry (block the request, retry with backoff, respond only when resolved) versus async queue + webhook (respond immediately with pending, resolve out of band). Async is the better fit here — a payment timeout is by definition already a slow path, and blocking the customer's request on a second network round-trip to the processor just risks a second timeout.

Left for the next level down: backoff schedule and max-attempts count, and what happens on exhaustion (dead-letter queue, alert, manual review) rather than silently giving up.

That needs an external dead-man's-switch — a separate watcher (cron or monitoring check) comparing each tenant's last-persisted cycle timestamp against a five-minute-plus-slack threshold.

That's the fork: everything driven by `govern()`'s inputs/state moves into the pure core as data; the one condition about the core's own absence has to live outside it.

A trigger fires on every write regardless of origin.
- **Actor identity crosses into the trigger via a session variable.** Triggers have no notion of "who's logged in," so `db.write()` (`db.js:16`, right after `BEGIN`) does `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = $1, app.request_id = $2` before running the caller's query; the trigger reads them with `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)`. `SET LOCAL` is transaction-scoped, so it can't leak across pooled connections.

The core fix isn't retry logic — it's that a timeout means "unknown," not "failed." Right now you're mapping unknown to failed and telling the customer, which risks a wrong message and (if you retry naively) a double charge.

What object storage and backend stack are you on? That decides the presigned-URL and queue mechanics.

Alerting has two shapes in SPEC.md, and they don't fit the same mechanism.

Four conditions map directly onto `result.guardrail` from a single cycle (`quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`) — these just extend the existing `if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded": alert(...)` line in the pseudocode with more branches, fired from the supervisor after each `govern()` call, same as today.

The other three are multi-cycle or absence conditions govern() can't see on its own, since it's pure and stateless about the clock:
- `feed_stale` past three cycles: the three-cycle count already has to be tracked somewhere for the "fall back to default cap" behavior in the guardrail itself, so it naturally lives in the persisted controller `state` and the supervisor alerts when that counter hits 3.
- Cap pinned at a band edge, and pace error >15%, for two consecutive cycles: neither changes govern()'s decision, so stuffing them into `state` would leak observability-only bookkeeping into the core. Cleaner to track these as small per-tenant counters in the supervisor layer, derived from the last two persisted cycle records, not part of govern()'s contract.
- Heartbeat missed: nothing inside the loop can report its own absence. This needs an external watchdog — a dead-man's-switch check on the "record the cycle" timestamp per tenant, alerting when it goes stale, run outside the 5-minute loop entirely.

The one fork worth deciding explicitly: alert on edge (state transition into the condition) vs. level (every cycle the condition holds). Several of these guardrails persist for hours once tripped (`quota_exceeded` holds at zero until day-roll, `floor_unreachable` holds at max) — firing `alert()` every 5 minutes for the whole duration would be noise. Edge-triggered, with a periodic re-notify (e.g. hourly) while still failing, is the standard pattern here.

Left for the next level: alert payload/schema, routing (who gets `config_invalid` vs `floor_at_risk`), and whether the supervisor-side counters for cap-pinned/pace-error get persisted (crash-safe) or live in memory (reset on supervisor restart).

Read through `db.js`, `auth.js`, and the two route files — the shape of this service makes the design fairly clean: `db.write()` in db.js:13 is already the single chokepoint every write passes through (it owns the only `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`), and `sessionUser` in auth.js already resolves every request to `req.user` before any handler runs. That's exactly the two pieces an audit trail needs.

**Recommended approach:** Postgres triggers do the capture, `write()` supplies the actor.

- Add an `audit_log` table (`table_name`, `row_id`, `action`, `actor_id`, `changed_at`, `diff jsonb` built from `row_to_json(OLD)`/`row_to_json(NEW)`) and an `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger on each audited table (`accounts`, `orders`, ...) that writes into it.
- Have `write()` run `SELECT set_config('app.actor_id', $1, true)` as the first statement inside its transaction, using `req.user.id` passed in from the route. `true` makes it transaction-local, so it resets automatically on commit/rollback — no leakage across pooled connections. The trigger reads it back with `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)`.
- Lock down `audit_log`: the app's DB role gets `INSERT` only, never `UPDATE`/`DELETE`, so the trail can't be edited after the fact — the compliance ask is "who changed what," which implies tamper-evidence, not just logging.

**The one fork worth calling out:** trigger-based capture vs. logging a row from inside each route handler. Handler-level logging is easier to read but silently breaks the day someone writes a migration, a psql one-off, or a new route and forgets the log line — it depends on every future call site remembering. Triggers make "for every write" structurally true regardless of what issues the SQL; the only thing the app layer has to guarantee is that `write()` sets the actor before the query, which it can do in one place since it's already the sole transaction boundary.

Left out: retention/partitioning for `audit_log` at volume, whether diffs need PII redaction before storage, and a read API for compliance to actually query the trail — worth a separate pass once the capture mechanism is agreed on.

Cache-aside with Redis, keyed by product ID, TTL as a safety net plus explicit invalidation on writes. On a request: check Redis, on miss hit the DB and populate the cache, on the product's update/delete path invalidate that key directly rather than waiting for TTL expiry — that's what keeps staleness bounded without needing a short TTL that would erase most of the benefit.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Granularity** — cache the raw DB query result vs. the fully rendered page fragment. Query-result caching still costs render time per request but composes cleanly if the page pulls from multiple tables; whole-page caching is faster but invalidates harder if any one input (price, inventory, reviews) changes independently. Given "nearly all of it is the database," cache at the query level first — it's the 900ms.
2. **Invalidation trigger** — TTL-only is simpler but trades staleness for simplicity; event-driven (invalidate on the write path) is correct but only works if all writes to product data go through code you control. If there's a bulk-import or admin-tool path that writes directly to the DB, event-driven invalidation will silently miss it, so that's the thing to check before committing to this design.

Key facts from the code: each box runs 4 worker processes with no shared memory (app.js:5-6), Redis is already the one thing every worker and every box has in common (redis.js:3-4), and the auth middleware in routes/api.js:9-19 already resolves `req.client.client_id` before any handler runs — and its own comment flags IP as an unreliable key since clients share NATs and use multiple addresses.

**Build it as a Redis-backed limiter keyed by `client_id`, as middleware in `routes/api.js` right after the auth block (line 19), before the route handlers.** Use a Lua script that does the read-check-increment atomically (`EVAL`) rather than separate `GET`/`INCR` calls — with 4 workers per box hitting the same Redis key concurrently, non-atomic check-then-act races let a client burst past the limit right at the boundary. Reject over-limit requests with `429` + `Retry-After`.

The one real fork: **fixed window (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`) vs. token bucket/GCRA.** Fixed window is a single Lua script and easy to reason about, but allows up to 2x the limit in a burst straddling a window edge. Token bucket avoids that and allows short legitimate bursts within budget, at the cost of a slightly more involved script (tracking last-refill timestamp per key). Given "hammering" reads as sustained abuse rather than a burst problem, I'd start with fixed-window — simpler, and upgradeable later without changing the key scheme.

Left out: whether to also throttle at the load balancer/gateway so an abusive client's requests never reach the app workers at all (protects CPU/connections, not just fairness) — that's the next layer down if app-level 429s aren't enough.

Poll, not push. `PLATFORM.md` rules out WebSockets and long-lived connections outright: connection upgrades 501 at the edge, functions are killed at 10s, and instances share no memory between invocations — so SSE would just be polling with extra failure modes anyway.

The one real decision is cadence, and the rollup job (`jobs/rollup.md:3`) already answers it: data changes once a minute, on the minute, from a single writer. So `public/dashboard.js` just needs its `load()` (dashboard.js:3-8) called on a `setInterval` instead of only on click and button-press — every 15-20s is enough to feel live without hammering an endpoint that's already cheap (`api/metrics.js:4`: 4KB/30ms). Compare the returned `computed_at` to the last-seen value before re-rendering, so a poll that lands between rollup writes doesn't cause a pointless re-render. Leave the refresh button wired to the same `load()` for people who want to force a check.

Depth I'm skipping: exact interval tuning, and whether to pause polling on a hidden tab (`document.visibilityState`) to cut idle load.

Root cause: `payments.js` sends no `Idempotency-Key` (PROVIDER.md line 20 flags this), and the vendor is explicit that a timeout means **unknown**, not failed — so today's only two safe outcomes are "don't retry" (current behavior, surfaces as a false failure) or "retry blind" (risk of double-charging). Fixing the message means fixing that gap, not adding a retry loop on top of it.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Where the idempotency key is generated and stored.** It has to be created *before* the first network call and persisted somewhere that survives a process crash — not just held in a local variable in `payments.js` — otherwise a retry after a restart generates a new key and you're back to double-charging. Simplest fit for this schema: reuse `order.id` as the key (or store a generated key on the `orders` row alongside `status`) at the top of the `/pay` handler, before calling `charge()`. Since an order only ever goes `pending` → `paid`, the key's natural lifetime matches the order's.

2. **What triggers a retry.** Only `req.on("timeout")` / network errors (unknown outcome) should retry — a 4xx from the vendor is a known decline and retrying it is pointless and slower for the customer. That means `charge()` needs to distinguish those two rejection paths (it currently collapses both into a generic `reject`), and the retry loop with backoff belongs around the timeout/network-error path specifically, capped at a small number of attempts, all resending the same key.

After that, `checkout.js`'s catch-all also needs to fork: retries exhausted with the vendor still unreachable is genuinely different from a decline, and probably shouldn't collapse into the same "payment failed" message or the same order status.

Left out: exact backoff/attempt-count values and what happens to the order status if retries are exhausted while the outcome is still unknown (e.g. a distinct status for manual/async reconciliation) — worth deciding once you know how the rest of the order state machine handles non-terminal states.

Recommendation: use Postgres full-text search — a generated `tsvector` column combining name and description, a GIN index on it, and `ts_rank` for ordering. No new infrastructure, and it's plenty for "type a few words, get matching products."

Two decisions fork this:

1. **Do you need typo-tolerance or instant-as-you-type results?** If yes, swap in a dedicated engine (Meilisearch, Typesense, or Algolia) — better relevance and speed, at the cost of running/syncing a separate service.
2. **How fresh must results be?** Postgres FTS updates are transactional and instant on write. An external engine needs a sync path (webhook on product save, CDC, or periodic reindex).

Left out at this level: ranking/weight tuning between name vs. description, the reindex pipeline if you go external, and debounce/pagination on the search box.

Recommendation: have the client request a presigned upload URL from your API, then upload the photo straight to object storage (S3/GCS/R2) from the phone — not through your app server. Phone camera photos run 3-15MB (more for HEIC/ProRAW), and proxying that through your API ties up request workers and risks timeouts on mobile networks for no benefit.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Client-side resize before upload, or accept raw and process after.** Resizing/re-encoding in the browser or app (e.g., cap at ~2000px long edge, convert HEIC→JPEG) before the presigned upload cuts upload time and storage cost dramatically, but adds client complexity and a slower path on old devices. If you skip it, accept raw and downsize server-side — simpler client, but you're storing and moving full-size originals.
- **Sync or async post-processing.** Thumbnails, EXIF stripping (phone photos carry GPS by default — strip it), and any moderation should run as a background job triggered by a storage event, with the listing showing photos as "processing" until done. Doing this inline on upload blocks the UI on mobile connections and re-couples the app server to the upload path you just decoupled it from.

Depth I'm leaving out: retry/resumability for flaky mobile uploads, per-seller rate limiting, and the moderation pipeline itself.

Derive alerts from the per-cycle record the supervisor already writes (tenant, guardrail, cap, pace_error, timestamp), rather than bespoke alert-firing code for each of the 8 conditions in the Observability section — `govern()` stays pure per the spec's own constraint, so the supervisor loop is the only place that can emit this. The single-cycle guardrails (`quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`) become simple "guardrail == X" rules against that record; the multi-cycle ones (`feed_stale` past three, cap pinned for two, pace error above 15% for two) become "count matching rows over the last N cycles" rules, evaluated by whatever monitoring stack you already run — which one is that?

Heartbeat-missed is the exception: a loop that isn't running can't alert on its own absence, so that one needs a dead-man's-switch check — something external verifying a fresh row landed in the last cycle interval — not a rule over the loop's own output. Schema for the record and the dedup/routing rules per guardrail are the next level down.

Two choke points already exist here and matter for this: `db.write()` at db.js:13 wraps every write in a transaction, and `sessionUser` at auth.js:5 resolves the actor on every request before any handler runs. Build the audit trail off both, not off the route handlers — a handler could always be added or a raw query run elsewhere and you don't want the audit trail to depend on remembering to log it.

**Capture "what changed" at the database, not the app.** Add an `audit_log` table and an `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger on each audited table (accounts, orders, ...) that writes `table_name, row_id, action, old_row, new_row` (as JSONB, via `row_to_json(OLD)`/`row_to_json(NEW)`) and `changed_at = now()`. This is the part that actually satisfies "for every write" — it fires regardless of which code path did the write (this service, a future service, a one-off migration, someone at a psql prompt), which an app-level log wrapping only `db.write()` can't guarantee.

**Get "who" to the trigger.** The trigger can't see `req.user`, so the transaction has to hand it a value: `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = '<id>'` right after `BEGIN` in `db.write()` (db.js:16), and the trigger reads it back with `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)`. To avoid threading `req.user` through every `db.write()` call site in accounts.js/orders.js, set it once via `AsyncLocalStorage` in `sessionUser` (auth.js:5) and have `db.write()` read it from that store — no call-site changes needed, and it fails closed (missing actor context = null, which stands out in review rather than silently mislabeling).

**Make it tamper-evident.** Revoke UPDATE/DELETE on `audit_log` from the app's DB role so a compromised app or malicious insider can't edit history — grant it INSERT-only. If compliance needs it to survive a DB-admin-level compromise too, ship rows to an external append-only sink (e.g. stream to S3) as a second measure.

Left out of this sketch, worth deciding separately: the `audit_log` schema/indexing for querying by row or by actor, retention and export policy, whether any columns (e.g. billing_email) need redaction before logging, and read auditing if compliance ever asks for that too.

The fork that matters: is the page identical for every visitor, or personalized (per-user pricing, inventory, "in your cart")?

- **Same for everyone** → cache the rendered page at the CDN/edge (Cloudflare, Fastly, etc.), keyed by URL, TTL a few minutes, purged on product update via webhook. This skips your app server entirely, not just the DB — bigger win than an app-level cache if it applies.
- **Personalized** → cache at the data layer instead: Redis/Memcached, cache-aside pattern keyed by product ID (`product:1234`), app checks cache first and falls through to DB on miss. TTL as a backstop (a few minutes) plus explicit invalidation on writes — when a product's price/stock changes, delete or update that key rather than waiting for TTL expiry, since stale price/stock is the failure mode that actually matters here; staleness on less critical fields (description, reviews count) can just ride the TTL.

Depth I'm leaving out: cache stampede protection (lock or early-refresh so a hot key's expiry doesn't send a thundering herd at the DB), and whether reads are dominated by a long tail of distinct products (low hit rate, cache helps less) versus a hot set of popular items (high hit rate, cache helps a lot) — worth checking your access pattern before picking TTLs.

Recommendation: token-bucket rate limiting keyed by `client_id`, enforced in Redis, applied as middleware right after the existing API-key lookup in `routes/api.js`.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Where the counter state lives.** `app.js` runs 4 cluster workers per box with nothing shared in module scope, and there are multiple boxes behind the LB — an in-memory counter only sees one worker's slice of a client's traffic, so the offending client could burst 4x (or more) past any per-process limit before anything trips. Redis is already the one thing every worker and every box share (`redis.js`), so the bucket has to live there, not in-process.
2. **Bucket algorithm.** Token bucket over fixed/sliding-window counters, so a client with legitimately bursty traffic isn't punished for a momentary spike, only for a sustained rate above its plan's refill rate. Implement it as a single Lua script (`EVAL`) in Redis so the read-refill-decrement-write cycle is atomic — with 4+ workers hitting the same key concurrently, anything less than atomic will race and let extra requests through right at the threshold.

Concretely: key `ratelimit:{client_id}`, script does refill-by-elapsed-time then decrement-if-available, size/refill rate driven by `req.client.plan` (already fetched). Middleware sits after the existing key-lookup middleware (needs `req.client`) and before the route handlers hit Postgres — that ordering is what actually shields the DB pool, which is the shared resource the hammering client is degrading. On empty bucket: `429` + `Retry-After`.

Left for the next level down: the actual limit numbers per plan tier, and whether `api_keys` lookup itself needs caching — right now every single request, rate-limited or not, does a Postgres round-trip in that middleware before the bucket check would even run.

Server push is off the table here: PLATFORM.md rules out WebSocket upgrades (501 at the edge) and long-lived connections (instances freeze between invocations, no sticky routing to pin a client to one). That leaves client-side polling as the only option.

Since `rollup` only changes once a minute (jobs/rollup.md), reuse the existing `load()` in `public/dashboard.js` and call it on an interval instead of only on click/load:

```js
window.addEventListener('load', load);
document.getElementById('refresh').addEventListener('click', load);
setInterval(load, 20000);
```

Two decisions that actually fork this:

- **Interval length** — 20-30s bounds staleness to well under the 1-minute rollup cadence without meaningfully increasing DB load (`currentRollup` is already a cheap 30ms query). Polling every minute exactly would risk aliasing against the job's own schedule and showing stale data half the time.
- **Pause when tab is hidden** — add a `visibilitychange` listener to stop the interval when the tab isn't active, otherwise every open dashboard tab burns a serverless invocation every 20s forever, including ones nobody's looking at.

Left out: exponential backoff on fetch failure, and whether `computed_at` should be checked client-side to skip a re-render when the rollup hasn't actually changed since the last poll.

The current code turns any timeout into an immediate `502 payment failed` (`routes/checkout.js:29`), and `payments.charge()` never sends an `Idempotency-Key` even though Cardstream supports one (`PROVIDER.md`). That combination is what makes retrying unsafe right now: per `PROVIDER.md`, a timeout means the charge state is *unknown*, not failed — it may have already been authorized. Retry blindly without a key and you risk double-charging; don't retry and you eat the "few times a day" as lost sales for no reason.

So the design has one load-bearing decision: generate the idempotency key **before** the first attempt and reuse it on every retry of that same charge. Store it on the order row (e.g. `idempotency_key` column) at the top of the handler, so a retry — even after a process restart — replays the same key and Cardstream returns the original charge instead of authorizing twice.

The second fork is where the retry loop lives:
- **Inline in `payments.charge()`**: catch the timeout, retry N times with backoff (a few seconds, capped), same idempotency key, still within the HTTP request/response cycle. Simple, but the customer's browser is holding a connection open for the duration.
- **Async via a job**: `checkout.js` writes the order as `status = 'charging'` with its idempotency key and returns immediately (e.g. "processing"); a worker retries the charge out-of-band and flips the order to `paid`/`failed` when it resolves, with the client polling or getting a webhook/push. More moving parts, but doesn't block the request and survives a server restart mid-retry.

Either way, only retry on timeout/network error — a definitive 4xx (card declined) should still surface immediately, not retry.

Left out: exact backoff/attempt-count tuning, and how the client learns the outcome if you go async (poll vs. websocket vs. webhook) — those are implementation details once you've picked inline vs. async.

Postgres full-text search, not a separate search service — 38k rows growing by a few hundred a month is nowhere near the scale where Elasticsearch/Algolia earns its operational cost, and you're already on Postgres 16.

Add a generated `tsvector` column combining `name` (weighted higher) and `description`, with a GIN index:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

New route mirrors `GET /` but adds `WHERE active AND search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)`, ordered by `ts_rank(search_vector, query)`.

The one real fork: plain `to_tsvector` matches whole words and handles stemming ("shoe" matches "shoes"), but won't help with typos or partial/prefix matches ("hoodi" won't match "hoodie"). If the product spec wants typo-tolerance or as-you-type matching, that's `pg_trgm` with a GIN trigram index instead (or alongside), which is a different query shape (`similarity()`/`%` operator) and a different index. Worth pinning down with product before writing the migration — full-text alone is the simpler build and likely sufficient for a first cut.

Route it around nginx, not through it. `nginx.conf:12` caps every body on that listener at 1m for PCI reasons on the payments endpoint, and per-location overrides were explicitly declined — a phone photo (typically 2–8MB) would just get rejected there, and that limit isn't going to move. `storage.js:10-16` already has the fix half-built: `signedUrl` supports `method: 'PUT'`, unused today, and CORS on the bucket already allows PUT from `market.example.com`. So the shape is direct-to-S3 upload:

1. Seller's client asks the app for a signed PUT URL for a new photo key (a new route calling `storage.signedUrl(key, {method: 'PUT'})` — mirrors the existing `/invoice` GET-URL pattern).
2. Client PUTs the image bytes straight to S3 with that URL, bypassing the app server and nginx's body limit entirely.
3. Client confirms success back to the app, which calls `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` to append to `listings.photo_keys` — this confirm step is required because the S3 PUT never touches the backend, so nothing else populates that column.

The one real fork: a bare presigned PUT has no size cap, so nothing stops an oversized upload once it's off nginx's leash. If that matters, use a presigned POST with a `Content-Length-Range` policy condition instead of PUT, enforced by S3 itself. Left out: content-type/EXIF validation, multi-photo ordering, thumbnailing, and deletion — worth a separate pass once the upload path itself is settled.
